Specifically, we find that the standard deviation of estimates converges to a stable value independent of the number of features, whereas the bias of estimates becomes minimizable. These findings may have applications in topics such as panel data analysis and regression with high dimensional temporal features.

Speech enhancement, a vital component in audio signal processing and the foundation for other advanced technologies like speech recognition and synthesis, is extensively researched. This paper showcases a novel deep learning architecture, centered on a comprehensive attention mechanism within a bidirectional neural network. This innovative design deviates from conventional attention-based models that often apply complicated memory modules and limited contextual information, whereas our proposed framework leverages contextual information from both distant and nearby past and future input elements. Through rigorous experimentation on the WHAM! dataset, our model demonstrates superior performance compared to established deep learning and attention-based models.

A negative pressure room (NPR) in biolabs and infectious-control hospitals must meet stringent safety standards set by bio-safety levels (BSLs) to prevent potentially deadly pathogens from escaping into the surrounding environment. These facilities maintain negative air pressure relative to the outside space by using specialized systems to contain the microbes. Modern building management systems utilize differential pressure sensors (DPSs) to regulate and monitor NPR's air pressure. Our research reveals a non-intrusive vulnerability in these systems, where an attacker can induce resonance in DPSs using malicious audio at their natural frequencies, causing the sensors to malfunction. Our findings show that the resonant frequencies of most DPSs fall within the range of human hearing. We have demonstrated that we can design music capable of generating these resonant frequencies and, in doing so, trigger a significant discrepancy in pressure readings. Our research shows that the malfunctions induced by this technique can fool the building management systems, potentially allowing pathogens to escape from NPRs. Our study also demonstrates that the resonant frequency-based attack can target multiple rooms simultaneously. Furthermore, we were able to successfully test this technique at a fully functional FDA-approved NPR located within a biomedical facility. Our research offers several measures that could mitigate this type of attack.

A key factor in microgrid operations is the capacity to store energy, but it also introduces new risks due to uncertainty about electricity demand and price. This study examines how a risk-averse decision maker allocates their storage capacity within a two-period decomposition framework. It reveals that the optimal storage allocation maximizes a risk-sensitive version of benefit-to-cost ratio, and this result has implications for renewable energy investors. Furthermore, the benefit of storage is affected by the level of price uncertainty.

In quantum systems, superpositions of electronic states rapidly evolve, 
within the timeframe of few femtoseconds to attoseconds, leading to a charge 
density that varies over time. This work takes advantage of newly produced, 
ultrafast soft x-ray pulses generated by an x-ray free-electron laser to create 
an excitation of core electrons in nitric oxide molecules. Additionally, 
application of an infrared laser pulse in a circular polarization enables the 
creation of a reference point, thus enabling us to study the temporal evolution 
of core electrons over several femtoseconds. A theoretical model accounting for 
electronic and nuclear motion as well as the internal field within the molecule 
provides a clear understanding of experimental observations. It shows that, due to 
the highly coupled relationships between electrons, nuclear motion causes a rapid 
shift in molecular levels, thus resulting in evolving internal fields within the 
molecule. It also results in the rotation of core electron states, thus affecting 
the temporal evolution of the decay. It may be necessary to incorporate this 
effect into the interpretation of experimental data from core-level spectroscopies 
using x-ray pulses.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which circulation patterns are mapped and classified. Notable patterns and trends emerge when varying rotation rate, as well as the rate at which heat and motion are transferred and released in the atmosphere. Similar patterns in circulation are found to occur under both laboratory and atmospheric conditions, when the curvature of the planet is considered. Baroclinic waves that behave similarly to those observed on Mars appear under specific conditions of temperature differences and atmospheric stability. Extremely fast planetary rotation leads to the formation of multiple jet streams on the poles, similar to the multiple jet patterns observed in gas giant atmospheres, and results in varying distributions of heat in the atmosphere with different rotation speeds.

Deep learning has seen significant advancements in recent years, with numerous challenges addressed through the application of multiple models. One such approach is semi-supervised learning, which combines small and large-scale datasets to train models. However, the standard evaluation protocol for SSL has generally been the use of labeled data alone, without considering the benefits of unsupervised data for a time-sensitive problem like few-shot learning. Few-shot learning learns new classes based on just a small number of labeled samples per class. In contrast, our research reevaluates the relationship between SSL and few-shot learning, highlighting the value of large-scale unsupervised data in informing model decisions and facilitating the learning of new classes. Through the modification of a popular metric, we demonstrate the ability to achieve up to a 5% improvement in the FLOPS of models with the same accuracy on the few-shot learning mini-imageNet benchmark. Our novel metric is called the dynamic learning scale, which gauges a model's ability to learn new classes based on the characteristics of both the model and the dataset. In addition, we introduce the concept of model fusion in few-shot learning, which involves the combination of models trained on both supervised and unsupervised data, allowing for the selection of the best model for each individual class. Through this approach, we are able to achieve up to a 12% improvement in the few-shot learning mini-imageNet benchmark, while simultaneously reducing the number of parameters by 20%.

This work offers a novel perspective on the complex eigenvalue spectrum of a specific class of non-normal operators, specifically Toeplitz operators, which are derived from the convolution form. The study establishes a connection between the algebraic multiplicity of an eigenvalue and the geometric properties of the relevant reciprocal operator, allowing for the calculation of multiplicity in some cases. The relationship between the operator's spectrum and the associated reciprocal operator's spectrum is examined, revealing conditions under which they are equivalent. The focus then shifts to analyzing the operator's singular values, determining conditions under than an eigenvalue lies on the boundary of the operator's spectral area, and exploring the link between the algebraic and geometric multiplicity of an eigenvalue. Finally, the article concludes with a discussion on potential future directions for specific types of operators, including Fourier transform and shift operators.

We suggest creating pairs of correlated bosonic states within a specific type of atomic system that includes dipolar atoms connected to an optical cavity. This system is characterized by having a large spacing between energy levels that allow for the implementation of a semiclassical approach. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this setup by showing how it can be used to generate two-state correlations in the form of a Michelson-like optical interference pattern. We also propose modifying the system to include a beam-splitter interaction that would enable the creation of squeezed states. Furthermore, we examine the potential for this system to be used in optical communications systems that rely on optical interference and demonstrate that even with the presence of atomic decay and other forms of loss, the system can still perform optical communications tasks efficiently.

Researchers who utilize silicon-based quantum computing need to comprehend the interactions between adjacent donors in silicon. These donors can be phosphorus atoms, which are used for quantum computing entanglement and state preparation. We utilized a multi-valley effective mass approach to accurately model the electronic properties of these donors. By integrating this approach with a 3D finite size simulation method, we simulated donor pairs in silicon with various orientations. Our results show that as the distance between donors decreases, so too does the energy difference, eventually converging to a value that aligns with previous research using simpler models. However, when the distance between donors is very small, certain energy levels become mixed due to the interaction of valence and conduction bands, resulting in increased energy differences. This occurrence varies based on the direction in which the distance between donors is measured, resulting in energy differences that differ by as much as 0.5 kHz. This variance presents a challenge for controlling the state of these donors and may impact the performance of quantum computing tasks such as interference and the preparation of certain entangled states.

Our investigation focused on the conductance of mercury telluride quantum wells at their gapless point, which has been previously difficult to study due to the challenge of achieving exact voltage balance in conventional transport measurements. Using an unconventional technique where the sample is treated as a part of the source-measure unit, we were able to overcome this limitation. Our findings show that, when the gate voltage is applied locally using a long, thin probe that also measures the conductance, we can accurately achieve precise voltage conditions. This method enabled us to collect a comprehensive set of data illustrating the conductance of Dirac fermions in mercury telluride quantum wells, particularly revealing the distinct peak structure associated with with edge channels and the influence of strain.

This research examines a novel adaptive cooperative Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) protocol called LACNAC, specifically focusing on its application in highway communication. By taking into account the unique characteristics of road traffic, particularly how vehicles at junctions tend to operate at a different speed from those on straight sections, the study aims to evaluate the performance of LACNAC in this context. An analytical model is developed to investigate the overall system behavior, and corresponding simulations are conducted to validate the results. Our findings reveal that the LACNAC system exhibits better overall performance compared to traditional cooperative NOMA and BC-NOMA protocols, characterized by increased throughput and reduced error rates in traffic areas with high intersection densities.

In our proposed approach, we develop a mathematical model that schedules operations for an dynamic time division duplexing system in fifth-generation cellular networks. Our model allocates time slots dynamically based on non-cooperative user connections' strategies. We analyzed the model's properties and derived a key insight that is applicable to solving dynamic scheduling problems. Additionally, our results indicate that cooperative connections can lead to significant increases in system performance. Furthermore, we investigate several special cases of the model, including an approach that utilizes a single time slot and an alternative method that enables inter-cell scheduling through resource sharing.

An analysis of a Hall anomaly in YBCO has been successfully replicated by incorporating the effects of migrating vacancies in a fixed lattice of vortices, and their interaction is quantitatively measured using BSCCO thin-film data.

Using experimental data from magnetization measurements in the Ising model with external field and temperature, researchers have determined the fixed point values of various moments that characterize magnetic fluctuations in the Ising transition. By analyzing susceptibility and magnetization at the critical point, they have found that fourth-order moments are consistent with the universal ratio predicted by universal scaling laws, whereas lower-order moments do not follow this prediction. Additionally, a new universal ratio emerges from comparing the magnetization at the critical point to the magnetization at the hysteresis loop's minimum, allowing it to be quantified for the first time. Furthermore, microcanonical signatures of first-order transitions are observed in magnetization measurements, specifically in hysteresis loops and magnetic polarization, which demonstrate the importance of including field in theoretical models.

A characterization of finite-dimensional commuting squares that generate a type of subfactor known as a superfluid is achieved, using a particular approach that involves a specific number of indices. Additionally, under an assumption related to index 3, a characterization of such squares is obtained, and it is established that they are equivalent to a specific type of matrix that represents a mutation in the ADE graph, which is a collection of points with lines connecting them.

In this work, we examine the capability of Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HamNNs) to acquire exact derivatives for their learned input-output relationships. To accomplish this, we first establish a straightforward Hamiltonian Neural Network model that operates like a straightforward function estimator. Subsequently, we investigate whether incorporating a Hamiltonian dynamics component enhances the training of these models when compared to conventional methods. To accomplish this, we devise two straightforward Hamiltonian learning procedures that leverage the unique properties of closed and fixed-point Hamiltonian dynamics. Fixing the point yields a novel Hamiltonian dynamic that is essentially equivalent to the HamNN's original objective, whereas fixing the closed point enables the separation of end-to-end Hamiltonian learning into two manageable components. Through our experiments, we conclude that HamNNs hold promise for efficiently learning exact derivatives with minimal supervision, especially when the data exhibits a linear underlying structure.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing users' confidence in it. A framework is proposed that includes multiple agents working together, one of which is a human who provides labels and receives feedback in the form of notification of correct and incorrect predictions. The human's trust in the model is assessed using a scoring system, and this score influences the updating of the model's parameters. Additionally, the human can select examples from the dataset to have them retouched, either by transferring features from similar instances that were labeled correctly, or through a random transformation. This method allows the model to learn from the human's preferences and adapt to their level of trust. The proposed strategy is tested on multiple datasets and demonstrated to improve the model's performance and the human's level of trust, as well as reducing the gap between these two metrics.

Detecting prohibited items in an x-ray image of luggage is crucial for ensuring public safety. However, the difficulty of interpreting medical imaging for those without prior training and the diverse range of prohibited items makes this task extremely challenging. Previously, convolutional neural networks (CNN) were attempted on this task, yet their limited success prompted us to develop a novel module that incorporates a unique lateral inhibition mechanism to enhance the network's performance. By integrating this module into a standard CNN framework, we achieved significant improvements and created a high-quality benchmark called HiBPS-B for evaluating the network's accuracy. Our innovative method consistently outperformed existing solutions and set new standards for the benchmark, achieving exceptional accuracy with only 7 layers. To ensure the benchmark's validity, we performed numerous experiments that validated the effectiveness of our method and established a top-performing model that achieved exceptional results and set a new standard for the benchmark.

We introduce a novel quantum invariant, dubbed $V_q$, for links in a thickened torus. This invariant is constructed using the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus, and it complements the range of properties common to other invariants of this type. Notably, tests of a conjectured relationship known as the Volume Conjecture yield supportive evidence. To facilitate computation, we also derive an alternative expression for $V_q$ based on a simplified expansion. This approach is particularly useful for examining the conjecture's implications in fields like topological quantum field theory. Moreover, we find that $V_q$ can be expressed as a sum of colored graph invariants, specifically the Khovanov-Rozansky homology, which provides a more intricate understanding of its behavior. Additionally, we investigate how $V_q$ relates to other invariants, including the Jones polynomial and superpolynomials. Finally, we examine the effects of various operations on $V_q$, including tunneling, stabilization, and satellite constructions.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine contextual information from various sources.  This study concentrates on enhancing Context-gloss Pair models, which incorporate contextual information along with a gloss to resolve word sense ambiguity.  Initially, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of these models under different training settings, involving both single and dual tasks, as well as an examination of the effects of adding noise to the glosses.  Our findings indicate that pre-training the WSD model on large-scale data with connected word sense tags is highly beneficial, and that incorporating noisy glosses in the training data leads to improved performance.  We further propose an unsupervised approach to obtain context-gloss pairs from Wikipedia, along with a related WordNet sense tag.  This context-gloss pair data is used to train an unsupervised context-gloss model, and our experimental results demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on three standard WSD datasets when using this approach.

This paper formulates a genuine integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function in terms of a specific combination of Cauchy principal integrals. To achieve this, the model is transformed into a form that allows for the application of famous results related to the uniqueness of the analytic extension of functions beyond their original domain. Additionally, the paper also obtains a revised integral expression involving a hypersingular integral.

This paper investigates top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions at 13 TeV and above, using the large acceptance and sensitivity of the LHC, specifically with the CMS detector. We examine the feasibility of identifying top quark pairs using several final state observables and signal-to-background ratios, ultimately determining the optimal conditions for detecting top quark production. Additionally, this study provides production cross-section estimates in proton-nucleus collisions, converting them into proton-proton collision cross-sections in proportion to proton-proton cross-sections, which are widely reported.

This study focuses on key elements in text-to-SQL tasks, specifically schema and semantic interpretation. We're exploring a novel aspect, implementation on real-world platforms, and addressing a pressing issue in research. To achieve this, we've developed a innovative method called $CTG^2$, a technique to leverage existing tools and overcome the divide between language models and database management systems. This approach can be seen as both a method to improve semantic interpretation in text-to-SQL tasks and a means to create more realistic evaluation benchmarks. We've conducted extensive testing of $CTG^2$ on both small-scale and large-scale datasets, proving its effectiveness and ability to bridge the gap between research and real-world applications.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy (DP) within analysis of network data, presenting fundamental concepts, an overview of current methods for processing private multi-node data, and a summary of research employing DP on graphs and networks. Additionally, it highlights prominent challenges and future directions for this field of study.

The vast image and instrumentary resources that Euclid will utilize to study cosmological phenomena, including optical and near-infrared imaging and spectroscopy, as well as a stellar reference catalog, will produce an immense amount of data requiring significant preservation efforts. Euclid's heritage potential is expected to significant, with scientific advancements and newly generated data offering opportunities for educational and educational community engagement. Nonetheless, the most substantial heritage aspect of the mission will be the extensive collection of optical and near-infrared images of approximately 2 billion high-redshift galaxies, which will be made accessible to the research community through the Euclid Heritage Portal. This portal will serve as a central platform for heritage-related activities, encompassing heritage-related operations, resources, and legacy data to be generated by the mission.

In this research, we propose an automatic method to generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a driving task that an equipped vehicle must perform. Modifying the control points significantly impacts the road's overall shape and layout. Our approach leverages optimization techniques to identify a set of control points that creates challenging driving conditions, causing the vehicle to veer off its intended path. We validated our method with three distinct search configurations, focusing on balancing testing speed and practicality for simulated evaluations of autonomous lane-keeping systems.

To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating engaging audio descriptions. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which annotates playlists with textual summaries that capture their musical content. To achieve this, a novel model is proposed that leverages multiple audio features and incorporates a semantic analysis of the playlist through a collaborative filtering component. The model is trained and evaluated on a large scale, demonstrating its capability to effectively summarize playlist content.

Researchers have successfully used quantum hydrodynamics to model non-equilibrium situations for quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel approach that directly generates random quantum hydrodynamic descriptions for interacting Bose gases. This method eliminates the need to establish a correspondence between microscopically described interactions and the macroscopic behavior as seen in quantum hydrodynamics. Instead, we set out the parameters of a random quantum hydrodynamic kernel that is consistent with established properties of the Bose gas, specifically its thermodynamic properties and correlation functions. We show that for a specific class of interacting Bose gases in a one-dimensional setup, we can precisely determine the quantum hydrodynamic kernel. Furthermore, we've developed a systematic approach to evaluate the predictions made by this method, comparing them with existing quantum hydrodynamic descriptions that have been rigorously derived. We find that our method is robust and gives reliable results, even when the quantum hydrodynamic kernel is complex and cannot be predicted analytically. We've specifically examined a one-dimensional interacting Bose gas in a harmonic potential and found that our method successfully predicts the transition from a state with mixed phase to a stationary state, in close agreement with existing quantum hydrodynamic descriptions that have been precisely derived.

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. The source code of our method has been made publicly available at https://github.com/cg1177/DCAN.

The theory of edge localized modes is based on the obstruction of an ECR flow by dividend walls, leading to a phase shift in the plasma edge and the generation of plasmoid filaments. PTM, occurring during major disruptions, originate from the diversion of an ECR flow by an intra-louver plasma patch, resulting from magnetic fluctuation effects. This causes a 300 degree angle rotation of the plasma edge and the formation of plasmoid filaments, characterized by magnetic fluctuation signatures and particle and heat transport channels.

This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for multiple mobile robots moving at high speeds in an unpredictable environment. Our approach leverages dynamic vortex potential fields to create local reference frames, allowing each robot to make independent decisions and adjust its path to ensure a safe distance from others, even if they have limited sensory input. We test this method with a variety of scenarios, including situations where the robots are moving at high speeds and in narrow passages. Our results demonstrate that our approach converges quickly and remains effective in dynamic situations.

Consider a long sequence of letters generated from an arbitrary source, assuming that the source complies with an ergodic, single-parameter family of stationary distributions. Given this setup, multiple sequences of a fixed length can be obtained by drawing independently and randomly from the source. For a given sequence length and underlying parameter value, the distribution of these sequences is examined as the sequence length increases, and a corresponding large deviation principle is proven. Similarly, a large deviation principle is established for averages of individual letter types within the sequences. Additionally, rate functions are derived that characterize the asymptotic behavior of averaged sequences and facilitate quantitative analysis of their deviations. The specific cases of binary and categorical sources are also explored in detail.

Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the potential benefits of Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRSs). Comprised of passive reflective components that can dynamically adjust their reflection properties, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of incident waveforms. This capability creates opportunities for complex signal processing tasks, such as target parameter estimation in radar systems, to be accomplished more efficiently. We investigate the application of an IRS in radar systems, highlighting its effectiveness in optimizing waveforms and enhancing the performance of target parameter estimation at multiple radar locations. Our results indicate that an IRS can increase the success rate of target parameter estimation, reducing it to 0.5 from 50%, and facilitate accurate estimation in scenarios where it is previously unfeasible. Furthermore, the implementation of an IRS is associated with negligible additional computational costs.

Fuzzers are widely used testing tools for robustness, exploiting innocent-looking inputs to uncover and exploit subtle flaws in software. Despite their benefits, traditional fuzzers have limitations when dealing with modern vulnerabilities such as logic flaws and memory-related issues. In contrast, focused testing, a more recent approach, aims to detect specific types of errors. However, evaluating the effectiveness of focused testing against traditional fuzzers remains unclear due to the lack of objective criteria for measuring performance. In this paper, a comprehensive evaluation framework is introduced, considering multiple metrics to assess the accuracy, thoroughness, and efficiency of testing. Utilizing this framework, a comparison is made between four leading fuzzers and a focused testing framework, with the findings highlighting the strengths and weaknesses of each testing method. The research demonstrates that focused testing can achieve superior results, surpassing the performance of traditional fuzzers in certain situations. The advantages of focused testing, including its potential to uncover a greater variety of flaws and require significantly less input data, are also illustrated.

Pretrained models are typically used in learning scenarios that mimic how data is experienced in real-world situations. Yet, we've observed that these models often aren't chosen based on their performance in continuous learning. In this study, we challenge this selection practice by demonstrating that a basic approach that doesn't utilize pretrained models surpasses the performance of methods utilizing such models in tasks that involve learning in sequences. Our method involves using a constant number of neurons to represent different data sets, while utilizing a fixed number of layers for all sequences. Additionally, we've discovered that employing few-layer models is effective, as it helps prevent the accumulation of misclassification errors. Our results show that this strategy yields notable improvements in cases involving large amounts of data, leading to short-term memory limits that challenge the use of pretrained models.

We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space, with respect to a given configuration on the surface's boundary. This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of surfaces with minimal area within specific homotopy classes in certain types of metric spaces. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between surfaces of minimal area and maps with minimal energy within certain homotopy classes, as well as those that satisfy a different 1-homotopy condition. This connection is key to our approach. We also show that when the surface in question is a sphere, there is a topological constraint limiting the possible configurations within a given homotopy class, especially regarding the configuration's 2-homotopy type.

This final installment concludes our comprehensive study of the solutions $u$ to the given semilinear parabolic equation on the real line. These bounded solutions $u$ of the equation $u_t = u_{xx} + f(u)$, where the initial data have multiple convergent limits, exhibit distinct boundary layer behavior as $t$ approaches infinity. Specifically, this research reveals that further along the solution trajectory, additional boundary layers emerge due to the instability of the equation, resulting in an alternating pattern of interior and boundary layer regimes. This analysis holds under the condition that the derivative of the function $f$ is sublinear.

Recent experimental findings in 64Ni suggest that a peculiar double shape configuration exists, where a spherical 0+ state and an asymmetric 0- state coexist. The asymptotic spherical 0+ state is primarily composed of protons occupying the Δn=2 spherical shell model orbitals, while the asymmetric 0- state is formed by protons in the δ-shell. Large basis dimension intrinsic wavefunction calculations were performed to investigate the 0+ and 0- states in 64Ni, and the results indicate that the monopole interaction plays a crucial role in driving the shape coexistence in 64Ni. The monopole interaction is found to significantly contribute to the formation of the δ-shell in 64Ni, and it facilitates the combination of the spherical 0+ state and the asymmetric 0- state to minimize the total energy.

Approximately nine years ago, Arad and Neeman established the concept of Lipshitz continuous games as a broader category that encompasses regular games, and proved a fundamental theorem stating that a wide range of bipartite lipshitz continuous games on the unit cube have efficient equilibrium payoff identification through just one round of six questions. Their discovery has far-reaching implications, given its relevance to various applications including the analysis of approximations in the evaluation of equilibrium points in octagonal games, and the potential for obtaining lower bounds on the number of queries required in more complex games. In a novel contribution, we address the question of whether the optimal one-round, four-question upper bound for bilipshitz continuous games can be surpassed, and in doing so, we introduce a novel technique that enables the development of lower bounds on the query complexity of specific classes of lipshitz continuous games. Our analysis demonstrates that the optimal one-round, four-question upper bound for bilipshitz continuous games can be surpassed, and in doing so, we provide the first known instance of a lower bound on the query complexity of a class of lipshitz continuous games.

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification.

Recently, neural network-based methods have excelled in various challenging tasks due to their exceptional performance in modeling complex relationships, yielding significant improvements in multiple applications. However, the extensive training required for these models on vast datasets to develop a desired skill or knowledge has become a major hindrance. To overcome this obstacle, the next generation of machine learning aims to achieve efficient knowledge learning by training neural networks in an autonomous and self-directed manner, similar to how humans naturally learn new skills. This goal has prompted researchers to explore training neural networks in an autonomous and self-directed manner by leveraging knowledge that is already inherent within the network itself. This is now being achieved through the use of neural network architectures that are instructional in nature, which provide personalized guidance to the network during training. This survey paper seeks to offer a comprehensive exploration of instructor-student neural network architectures that utilize knowledge that is implicit within the network itself. This involves examining the numerous variations of this type of architecture that have been developed across various knowledge learning applications and also discussing the critical aspects that have been identified in the research literature.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our approach, titled the "Brief Function," allows for a rapid determination of the Most Probable Explanation (MPE) and can also be utilized to address constrained optimization issues. We demonstrate that utilizing Brief Functions leads to a significant boost in computational performance, specifically in scenarios where exact MPE calculations are strenuous. We showcase the utility of our approach by applying it to two notable problems: Bayesian inference in probabilistic graphical models and Maximum Margin Learning. The key benefit of our approach is its ability to provide exact solutions, which is particularly valuable in settings where model interpretation and subsequent actions are based on the optimal solution.

The interaction between a laser beam and a cold gas of atoms is examined using single-beam absorption spectroscopy in a sample of ultracold strontium atoms. Measurements with varying laser frequencies and powers reveal the absorption of energy by the atoms as well as the transfer of momentum, which results in the recoil of photons as predicted by quantum mechanics. These interactions were thoroughly analyzed and are characterized by a system of equations that account for both momentum transfer and the recoil of photons. These equations can also be applied to other systems that involve the interaction of a laser beam with a cold gas of atoms.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of liquid materials undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from low viscosity to high viscosity behavior. Despite its prevalent nature, the underlying physics of shear thickening remains poorly understood, primarily because it is challenging to study beyond the point of initial transition. In order to gain a more comprehensive grasp, researchers incorporated a numerical approach that could model and simulate the dynamics of many individual particles interacting with one another. Utilizing this method for suspensions of rectangular particles in a variety of sizes and shapes, scientists were able to collect a vast amount of data covering nearly the entire range of transition. By examining these simulations in depth, the researchers discovered that the transition from low to high viscosity behavior occurs gradually and is controlled by a simple relationship that varies depending on the size of the particles. Interestingly, even when the particles are very large in ratio to the flow velocity, the behavior still follows the same rules established for smaller particles. Furthermore, it was found that viscosity can be divided into two distinct components: one that is influenced by the particle's surface area and volume, and another that is influenced by the particle's shape. The findings of this research have the potential to significantly advance our understanding of the physics behind shear thickening, and scientists believe that this knowledge could be applied to address other complex problems involving the interaction of particles in flows.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, particularly with respect to a specific embedding of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within a tensor product. As a result, the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be presented through generators and defining relations, which can be derived from those of the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$. The relationship between the Racah algebra and the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ expands our understanding of the latter, specifically providing its presentation, Hilbert series, and dimensional sequence. Furthermore, this connection may facilitate the determination of dimensions for the unitary irreducible representations of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, which constitute a key component in the dimensional sequence of the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$.

Our study shows that in a bilayer hexagonal magnet, low-lying triplon excited states may have a unusual behavior where they form a twisted superfluid or supersolid state, driven by both quantum fluctuations and inter-layer interactions. Using a quantum Monte Carlo method and a model that incorporates both effects, we found that the twisted superfluid and supersolid phases can be realized using zero-magnetization and anti-ferromagnetic conditions respectively. These findings can be observed in experiments through measurements of inter-layer triplon-trippon interactions and triplon condensation in the center of the Brillouin zone. Additionally, we discovered that applying an external strain can be used to control the twist angle in the twisted superfluid phase.

This study supplements our earlier research on WIMP-nucleus collision velocities-recoil angles distributions and recoil angles-spectra of final state particles. Here, we enhance the visualization of our findings by introducing three-dimensional plots of velocity-recoil angle correlations and spectra of scattered nuclei or particles for various angles. Our simulation considers 1 GeV WIMPs colliding with argon nuclei at rest and accounts for quark and gluon contributions using the PDF set CTEQ6. Our results demonstrate little variation in velocity-recoil angle distributions and spectra of scattered nuclei or particles when considering different angle settings. Furthermore, our analysis reveals significant differences in velocity-recoil angle distributions and spectra of scattered nuclei or particles when comparing the outcomes of scattering off spherical nuclei to those of real nuclei with shell structures.

An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the influence they have on retrieving all relevant information. The study's results show that a substantial number of the participants are unaware of potential biases in search algorithms and the possible strategies to prevent them from overlooking essential information. Notably, our data reveal that as much as 20% of the necessary information may go undetected due to the influence of Web search personalisation. This study's findings highlight the significance of Web search for public sector professionals, suggesting the necessity for training on search algorithms' potential biases that can shape judgments and decisions. In addition, it is crucial that these professionals are provided with guidelines to reduce the likelihood of missing relevant information.

We are presenting a comprehensive conceptual design for a cutting-edge TeV-scale muon collider with multiple capabilities, as well as a robust framework for delivering high-luminosity collisions with incredibly low initial energies. This report outlines the fundamental physics advantages of such a collider, emphasizing its immense potential in discovering new Higgs bosons and shedding light on mystery areas in the universe, such as neutrino mass creation. Additionally, it highlights the capabilities of this collider in enhancing our understanding of established particle physics theories and refining existing limits with an incredibly sensitive detector. Furthermore, we present a thorough, multi-disciplinary roadmap for realizing this visionary project, involving both the development of sophisticated technologies and the training of a skilled, diverse workforce.

A cutting-edge, high-performance imaging technique has been developed to photograph cross-sections of the body in detail. This technique acquires 3D data while accounting for movement caused by breathing, ensuring crisp and clear images. By making small adjustments to a certain parameter, images are re-created that accurately reflect static body parts and account for parts that move with breathing. This helps reduce noise and motion distortions in images. By testing this technique on real people, it was shown that it compares favorably to conventional imaging methods in terms of picture quality and comfort levels. Furthermore, it was found that certain parameters such as motion within the body and breathing patterns remained consistent over time, allowing for standardization of imaging protocols. This technique has the potential to photograph parts of the body in detail, reducing the need for invasive procedures.

This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing secure control systems for complex, nonlinear processes subject to input limitations. Specifically, it outlines the development of an Input Constrained Control Barrier Function, which pinpoints a safe operational area for the system and generates reliable feedback mechanisms to maintain the system within that area, even in the presence of unforeseen disturbances. The paper also establishes the connection between these constrained barrier functions and traditional Control Barrier Functions, while highlighting the critical role of function sparsity in achieving optimal system performance. Finally, the paper demonstrates the practical applicability of these concepts through the development of secure feedback and feedforward controllers for a nonlinear cart-incline system and a vertical takeoff aircraft.

In topology and geometry, geometric regions are often represented by equivalence classes of geometries, where specific transformation rules apply. To facilitate this representation, we introduce the concept of an ordered geometry and associated equivalence relations, and then develop the CF-approximation framework to derive unique geometric representations for each equivalence class. The CF-approximation framework involves combining ordered geometries using combination operators, and we show that this results in a topological space that is homeomorphic to the original geometry. The CF-approximation framework can be applied to develop metric and angle spaces that are equivalent to the original geometry, and we demonstrate this by deriving the equivalence classes for familiar geometric shapes, such as lines, planes, and spheres. Furthermore, we investigate the relationships between these classes and demonstrate that they conform to intuition. The CF-approximation framework provides a foundation for defining relations, such as inclusion and intersection, and we define an approximation order for comparing geometries and their corresponding classes. Additionally, we explore connections between the CF-approximation framework and other methods of geometry representation.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, the large number of possible permutations in NLP makes precise calculation challenging. As a result, existing methods fall back on approximate techniques such as the Bayesian approximation or the tail probability estimation. In contrast, our proposed framework provides a more accurate representation of the test statistic's distribution and offers a more reliable comparison of test results. This precise method enables a less biased evaluation of system performance and is particularly useful in identifying the best system among several options. Our analysis demonstrates that the standard Bayesian approximation can lead to biased results and shows how our technique performs better in several NLP tasks. Our framework is now part of the standard metrics evaluation tools used in several competition platforms.

A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for the six primary shipping routes. Furthermore, instructions on combining and verifying datasets are provided using the knowledge of shipping industry specialists and former top executives. A descriptive analysis of previously unstudied market phenomena known as the "container crisis" is conducted with this data. Structural changes in the data variables are then identified to demonstrate how the dissolution of shipping monopolies affected market behavior.

We define loom areas as a more general framework encompassing both leaf spaces and space of leaves in reference to leafed foliations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, we establish that there is a natural correspondence between loom areas and veering triangulations, thereby extending a prior correlation between leaf spaces and these triangulations.

Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of node interactions and graph connectivity. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Learned Sparsification, which extracts the most crucial edges for each neural network layer by assigning weights. By doing so, we impose a sparse constraint on the edge connections, facilitating the detection of important relational patterns. Our approach is agnostic to specific graph neural network models and easily integrates with existing frameworks. We demonstrate the efficacy of Learned Sparsification through visible pattern discovery and reduced training data in supervised graph classification tasks, leading to accurate results and enhanced interpretability.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more robust estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches.

Building on previous findings, we observed in Part I that compact, singular areas within a manifold of positive scalar curvature can be conformally deformed to reveal related minimal geometries sharing key characteristics. This deformation preserves features like Ahlfors regularity, Poincare inequality validity, and tangent cones with positive scalar curvature. In Part II, we employ surgery-style arguments to successfully remove the singular sets present in these geometries.

The Nernst effect is a comprehensive response to temperature and magnetic field changes, affecting all conductive materials and especially unusual phenomena observed in the liquid state near superconducting gaps. This study focuses on the vortex liquid state within a type-II superconductor and attempts to explain the anomalous Nernst effect through increased viscosity and a complex process involving both frozen and mobile entropy within the vortex liquid. Our investigation involves a combination of experimental and theoretical analysis, and we observed that the anomalous Nernst effect is closely related to the entropy distribution between the vortex core and the surrounding normal state. This distribution is influenced by the energy barrier at the core, and it plays a crucial role in determining the liquid's conductivity and magnetic properties.

Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a novel framework that enables real-time coordination and efficient management of aggregators by incorporating a new variable, real-time aggregate flexibility, in a model predictive control (MPC) context. Specifically, we develop an affordable and robust algorithm capable of estimating real-time aggregate flexibility in seconds, in contrast to traditional methods that require several minutes. This achievement facilitates more frequent and optimal management of aggregators and the grid as a whole.

The recent interest in the stock market can be attributed to growing inflation rates prompting people to invest in equities, commodities, and other assets, as opposed to saving. Deep Learning's ability to accurately predict time series data has been consistently demonstrated. In the realm of technical analysis, using indicators is the most widely adopted approach among traders and investors. Another essential aspect is sentiment analysis, reflecting the emotional state of investors' willingness to invest, where various techniques such as Machine Learning and Neural Networks have been employed. From simple linear regression to advanced neural networks, researchers and investors have experimented with multiple methods to forecast the stock market. It is evident from recent market fluctuations how news headlines and cryptocurrency prices are affected. This research paper presents an ensemble of state-of-the-art techniques to forecast stock values. It starts with applying a BERT-based sentiment analysis model to analyze the emotional state of Apple Inc investors listed on NASDAQ. A subsequent GAN-based model predicts the company's stock value based on technical indicators, global stock indexes, commodity prices, and historical prices along with the sentiment scores. This model's performance is compared to benchmark models including LSTM, GRU, vanilla GAN, and ARIMA.

When a perturbing planet interacts with a varying internal pressure of a star or solar mass object, its Keplerian orbit is disrupted, resulting in velocity variations in the planet's motion. Currently available theories fail to accurately account for the complex surface conditions of these objects, often assuming a constant density to simplify calculations. In our new formalism, we've developed a comprehensive set of equations that take into consideration the effects of internal rearrangement within these objects, allowing for a more precise calculation of the induced tidal forces and resulting orbital patterns. Using these equations, we've derived a new universal envelope formula that provides a clear and concise representation of the relationship between tidal forces, density, and radius. This new formula holds significant value for its broad applicability, encompassing both stars and solar mass objects, and is a crucial advancement in the field, given the need for more precise calculations in recent studies. In the context of the SC-CAT project, this new formula is key to validating the circularization models used in the analysis and could also be employed in the analysis of planetary transits in scenarios where the planet is in a highly eccentric orbit.

In this research, we examined double Higgs production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the context of the Standard Model and its variations. The study considered the impact of two types of new physics: first, new heavy particles affecting Higgs boson interactions; and second, Higgs interactions involving leptoquarks. The analysis focused on Higgs decay to bottom quarks, one of the most challenging processes to measure. Using Precision Tools and SPhEnIC, our calculations considered all relevant processes, initial states, and BSM models, and explored how predicted signals relate to theoretical parameters and actual measurements. Our findings revealed how predicted signals depend on BSM models, Higgs couplings, and energy scales, and highlighted the importance of considering BSM effects when interpreting future experiments. However, we also found that, in some cases, predicted measurements may deviate from actual measurements if BSM effects are significant. The study suggested that, to fully understand future measurements, BSM effects should be considered, and that this should motivate further research into BSM models.

Various modifications of general relativity can be distinguished by
the nature of their kinematic and dynamical properties.  In this study, we
concentrate on theories that modify gravity by altering its dynamical
properties while maintaining its geometric structure, and we derive a new,
general form for the Lagrangian that represents these theories.  Our new
lagrangian takes the form $R + f(R,\,R_{\mu\nu}R^{\mu\nu})$, and within this
framework, we derive the explicit forms of Einstein-Dilaton gravity and
Brans-Dicke gravity when the parameter $beta$ is equal to $-(1/2)$ and derives
the known form of $f(R,\,r)$ gravity when the function $f$ is a linear form.

A new computational framework is introduced to speed up the calculation of localized shocks in a five-dimensional space that mimics anti-gravity, by simplifying the complex Einstein equations. It's discovered that using a first-order approximation yields highly accurate results, which can be broken down into two manageable sets of equations. Further, it's observed that one set has minimal impact on boundary measurements, allowing the calculation to be streamlined. This improvement results in significantly faster numerical solutions, with minimal errors, at roughly one-tenth the original time for specific conditions.

We investigated the flow of a fluid through a layer of granular material with a long, thin cylindrical obstacle moving through it. The study focused on how the shape of the cylinder affects resistance as it moves. By examining various angles, we found that the shape of the obstacle that creates the greatest obstacle varies depending on the speed at which it moves. There are two significant angles: one creates the greatest obstacle when moving quickly and the other when moving slowly. These findings challenge current theories of particle flow and could be applied to move large objects through a bed of grains.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the mass of new stars formed, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be converted into stars due to outflows. Our findings suggest that outflows impose a critical regulatory mechanism on the conversion of gas into stars, potentially having a broader impact on the galaxy's evolution.

Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area with the use of Bayesian optimization methods, which can quickly evaluate points in the search space by exploiting costly evaluations. However, these methods have limitations when dealing with a high number of variables, particularly in scenarios where each evaluation provides a comprehensive system log that contains valuable information for future evaluations. In response to this issue, we propose a novel approach called BoGraph that leverages graph neural networks to model the relationships between system components from log files. By incorporating this model into Bayesian optimization, BoGraph enables the discovery of exceptional configurations in multiple areas, outperforming established methods by up to 2 times.

Our research examined the triangular flow's origin within a multiphase transport model, applying it to both Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at various energies. Despite initial $v_3$ increases with energy, our analysis revealed that triangular flow is heavily influenced by initial conditions and is not inherently energy-dependent. However, when considering particle ratios such as $p_{{\rm T}}$ spectra and mean values, we observed significant energy dependencies that align with experimental data, suggesting that triangular flow may be interlinked with other flow components.

Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine access and interconnection.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityAssessment is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality evaluation pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, has been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies.

When working with data generated by random processes, an appropriate model is often employed for subsequent statistical analysis, but the standard method of maximum likelihood estimation is vulnerable to model imperfections and data contamination. As alternative methods without assumptions about a specific model typically lose efficiency, this paper introduces a robust parameter estimation method suitable for discrete data sets based on a flexible model that incorporates leeway for model deviations. Formulated within the context of a general statistical framework, this method yields consistent and asymptotically normal estimates under mild conditions, and can be computed using established software. As a result, traditional inference techniques remain applicable.

This study presents new findings from the Oyster campaign, focusing on photoionization processes in the massive outflows of two distant Seyfert galaxies. Initially, we observed radial metallicity variations in these galaxies, with enhanced [NII]/Halpha ratios observed at greater radii. However, when analyzing radial gas flows in these galaxies, our results revealed unexpectedly high [OIII]/Hbeta ratios at certain angles, indicating over-ionization which couldn't be explained by the central active galactic nucleus. To illustrate this phenomenon, we utilized detailed 1D models, confirming that gas in these galaxies is subject to photoionization due to the AGN. Notably, this over-ionization is more pronounced at angles greater than 45 degrees, which we attribute to increased gas density at the edge of broad line region and potentially, enhanced gas velocities in these regions.

As IoT systems grow, complex applications at the edge require more efficient processing, as high data volumes necessitate improved processing power.  Despite the speed benefits of processing data closer to its source, there are costs associated with deploying applications at the edge, limiting the types of analyses that can be performed.  To strike a balance between processing speed and application deployment costs, a new approach called Event-Driven Evaluation (EDE) has been developed, allowing user-specific events to trigger specific program elements, reducing unnecessary computation and leading to faster, more efficient processing.  Three real-world use cases - traffic monitoring, a wearable fitness tracker, and a smart home system - demonstrate the EDE's effectiveness, showing it can achieve significant performance benefits and lower energy consumption with minimal additional memory requirements.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has obtained precise data which is being used to study rare and unusual occurrences in the world of subatomic particles, specifically within a family known as beauty mesons. By analyzing these events with a level of detail never before possible, researchers are exploring fundamental questions about the behavior of particles and the nature of matter. For example, a phenomenon called CP violation, where certain observations differ from their mirror images, is being studied to determine its overall occurrence rate. Additionally, the study of beauty mesons also offers insights into two extremely rare events involving the beauty quark, namely the muon plus a small amount of energy being released from a particle called a D meson, and the decay of a D meson into a muon and a particle called a meson.

The generation of realistic traffic scenes through automation holds significant potential for expanding and refining semantic segmentation datasets, especially in regions where data is limited. To achieve this automation, we introduce SceneGen, a traffic scene generation model based on GAN technology, which is trained on real-world datasets, such as CityScapes. SceneGen's primary objective is to create more realistic and varied traffic scenes by generating specific elements, such as shapes and textures, for common traffic objects, such as cars, bicycles, and trees. In order to evaluate SceneGen's performance, we develop a metric called Traffic Quality Score (TQS), which assesses the realism and diversity of generated scenes. TQS takes into consideration both the visual appearance of individual objects and the overall scene composition. We discovered that SceneGen not only produces significantly more realistic and diverse scenes than a baseline approach but also achieves this through efficient learning, with notable improvements in TQS score across multiple trials. Moreover, SceneGen is particularly effective at generating scenes with complex backgrounds, such as urban areas, and has a user-friendly interface that allows users to explore its capabilities and adapt the model to other traffic-related datasets.
On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic states that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation.

A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems.

A group of integers $a_n$ is considered ergodic with respect to a growth sequence $n_k$ if the formula $\lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n_k\le N}a_{n_k} = 0$ holds true for all possible $k$. We discuss what conditions must be met for a sequence $n_k$ that consists of multiple subsequences $n_h$, $n_g$ etc., for which the limits $h\to\infty$ and $g\to\infty$ yield ergodic results, to also yield an ergodic outcome $n_k\to\infty$.

We developed three-dimensional hydrodynamic models of superbubble formation to
study the early stages of superbubble growth from young coeval massive star
clusters located within low-metallicity ($0.02Z_{\odot}$) molecular clouds.
Specifically, we explored how pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
affect pair-instability SN clumps and superposed dense gas clumps within these
molecular clouds. Our computational simulations reveal that in environments where
low-metallicity pair-instability SNe dominate, there is an increased amount
of dust produced and a higher density of SN shocks within pair-instability SN
clumps due to their highly dense and cool characteristics. As a result, these SN
shocks experience increased levels of cooling, leading to a more significant amount
of dust growth within these clumps. Therefore, we expect that a substantial number
of dust clumps produced by such low-metallicity pair-instability SNe will be
ejected from their host molecular clouds at high velocities, potentially contributing substantially to the intergalactic medium's dust reservoir.

Our proposed Far3Det framework represents a groundbreaking achievement in 3D object detection for distant camera perspectives. As 3D labels become increasingly expensive to obtain to to inherent 2D-3D ambiguities, we've demonstrated that 3D annotations based on front-facing 2D labels can be more cost-effective while achieving comprehensive datasets. This is made possible by establishing a far-field 2D-3D correspondence where objects can be at least 10 times their diameter distance from the camera, offering a unique opportunity for research in this area. To support this work, we've introduced the FarField3D dataset, comprising 50,000 3D annotations for the KITTI dataset, and proved that a straightforward extension of existing 3D detection methods falls short. In response, we've developed Far3Det, a cutting-edge 3D detection framework that tackles this challenging problem by establishing a correspondence between 2D and 3D and employing a novel transformation technique to enhance 2D detection results. Our research shows that Far3Det achieves a remarkable 57.57% mAP at far-field distances, a 25.91% increase over the baseline method. Our code and dataset are available for download at https://github.com/Alibaba-Digital-Migration-Future/Far3Det.

This paper introduces a quantum machine learning model called UFlappY (UFY), which is trained to recognize and generate molecules that have stable, lowest-energy states. The model combines Unstructured Bond Space Representations and a Labeled Graph Neural Network to classify molecules based on their chemical properties. As part of our research, we showed that UFY can successfully identify well-known chemicals and substances that are easily found in everyday life, such as water and benzene. More importantly, the model was able to discover new, hypothetical compounds with low-energy states and characteristics, which are consistent with established chemical theories. Given its capabilities, our research suggests that quantum machine learning models like UFY have great potential to create new materials with desired properties, which could be challenging or even impossible using traditional methods.

Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration, which translates external imaging data to internal mapping information for operating robots. Because this process needs to account for multiple unknowns, traditional methods often incorporate prior knowledge about tissue behavior. For precise alignment, however, it's essential to consider the specifics of mechanical properties for specific tissues. Researchers have developed a method using machine learning to assign these properties during alignment. By doing so, they've achieved more accurate results than previous approaches, which only used generic property values, in experiments using real data from liver and kidney procedures.

For a stationary and spherical spacetime, the energy-momentum tensor allows for conformal regridding, leading to the possibility of identifying its conformal symmetries. The paper establishes that the conformal symmetries of this energy-momentum tensor are linked to the conformal regridding generators, along with the stationary flow, and a specific quartet of flows associated with the conserved currents derived from the conformal regridding process. It is further demonstrated that this quartet of flows can be represented by specific expansions in terms of the spherical basis vectors. The connection between the energy-momentum tensor's conformal regridding and its conformal symmetries is explored, along with a discussion on the implications of these findings for the Bianchi identities.

For Self-Supervised Scene Flow Estimation, we need to establish correspondences between two images taken in succession, relying on features that are learned automatically. However, the features gleaned from a training dataset, which often embrace diverse imagery, can be untrustworthy due to their potential to incorporate erroneous correspondences. This vulnerability creates an opening for crafted outliers to manipulate the metric learning process and impede flow estimation performance. To counter this challenge, we introduce a novel method that resists the influence of these anomalies while learning to establish correspondences. The proposed approach, which we've incorporated into a scene flow estimation framework, employs a unique form of implicit occlusion masking and uses a unique flow guidance field to exclude outliers and promote the learning of robust features. Through extensive testing, our method demonstrates superior performance compared to current self-supervised scene flow estimation methods and even surpasses baseline models that leverage optical flow techniques for training.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's effectiveness across real-world classification datasets.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, using the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields.

In this research, we address two primary problems associated with cubic graphs: finding a Hamiltonian cycle and determining a proper edge-colouring using three colours. We establish a key equivalence for a broad category of these graphs, specifically those that do not contain $K_3$ as an induced subgraph, and have a property that every set of five vertices contains a pair with a distance of at most two. This equivalence states that a graph in this category has a Hamiltonian cycle if and only if it has a proper edge-colouring using three colours. Additionally, we demonstrate that every such graph with this specific property can be obtained from a cycle by successively adding edges to it, effectively creating a process that maintains the desired property. Furthermore, we explore the implication of this equivalence on certain subgraphs within this category.

We examine a family of block arrangements in the Cartesian plane and establish a link to a specific polynomial, before using this connection to investigate the prime numbers within a certain range that can be expressed as the sum of four squares. Additionally, we identify specific prime values of this polynomial at particular points within the Cartesian plane.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can independently discover and enforce system call filters based on a existing code, without requiring manual configuration or code modification. This approach is particularly suitable for complex programs, especially those with shared code pathways, where instrumentation is difficult and time-consuming.
