We examined the DIS structure function $F_2$ in medium, interacting with the plasma via electromagnetic field interactions. By metabolizing the data with Monte Carlo methods, our results were compared to empirical findings from experimental analyses of deep inelastic scattering. Additionally, we explored the temperature dependence of the structure function $F_2$ within the quark-gluon plasma. Furthermore, our model was extended to incorporate the production of heavy mesons, providing insight into the creation of heavy flavor from the interaction of electromagnetic fields with the quark-gluon plasma.

Our proposed approach offers a novel view video prediction framework that builds on existing dual representation methods. Unlike previously reported work, our research demonstrates that view video prediction can be achieved through a dual representation model in which the target view is represented as the sum of two components: a background part and a foreground part. Our model establishes a dual representation for the target view by using two separate networks, one for each component. Unlike the conventional dual representation technique which uses a single network to determine the target view by weighing the parts, our approach trains the two networks independently to predict each component of the target view. Our model is then used to predict the target view by adding the two estimated components. We evaluated our approach using the MVGVR dataset, and the results show that our predicted frames outperform the current state-of-the-art algorithms, particularly for longer-term prediction frames.

In multi-level systems, inter-level coupling plays a significant role in magnetic properties and spin wave phenomena. This work involves the theoretical and experimental investigation of an equilateral triangle lattice composed of exchange-coupled diamond spin clusters, focusing particularly on the $|\Psi\rangle$ state. An experimental setup has been developed to measure the very small energy difference between two levels, achieving this through a combination of applied magnetic fields and precise timing in the optical preparation of the $|\Psi\rangle$ state. The energy difference was found to be as small as $2\pi\times 0.57$ MHz, and this very precise control over the system has the potential to contribute to quantum computing applications.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches using the same model and obtains similar outcomes. However, differences in the spectrum arise due to distinct parameter values, highlighting the need for more precise OBSERVATIONAL DATA.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our results from a detailed, well-mixed framework to those from a less complex model, we identified both to be mutually consistent and robust against variations in physical parameters, as well as changes to turbulence intensity and shape of the bus. Furthermore, our study provides a theoretically supported basis for the efficacy of seats arranged in a linear fashion, previously observed in experimental data, in reducing the transmission of airborne pathogens.

Future space-based missions such as QUBES and IACOBA will enable precise measurements of quantum properties in the vacuum, specifically quantum diffraction and birefringence, which are inherent to photons. As a result, researchers will need methods that can accurately detect these phenomena, potentially revealing new properties of nature. This study evaluates the effectiveness of conventional detection methods, including photodetector arrays, time-stampers, and Resonant Tunneling Devices, in detecting these phenomena. Depending on the frequency of incoming photons and the type of phenomenon to be measured, some detection methods prove more suitable than others. For instance, photodetector arrays demonstrate versatility, while time-stampers exhibit superiority in measuring extremely sparse photon fields. Additionally, Resonant Tunneling Devices show distinct advantages in measuring quantum diffraction and birefringence in massless and mass-sensitive configurations respectively. Furthermore, this evaluation highlights that nearly all detection methods can recover data lost due to the arrival time uncertainty of photons, potentially revealing the quantization of photon arrival times. Moreover, this analysis suggests that extremely precise measurements of these phenomena could provide new insights into the massless properties of photons and the interaction between photons and virtual particles.

In 1923, J.M. Eisenlohr and G.A. Farris developed a mathematical approach to defining the number of "faces" in a three-dimensional, transitive polyhedron. This method can be applied to determine the counts of edges, vertices, and faces in specific polyhedra, including triangular and quadrangular prisms. However, their method only works accurately for transitive polyhedra with regular n-gons.

Building upon our previous work, researchers have suggested various ways to enhance uncloneable encryption, a primitive that prevents two or more functions from producing identical outputs given their respective secret keys. Some proposed extensions aim to ensure output diversity even if an adversary has access to one of the functions and can manipulate its output. Others suggested using multiple independent random numbers in the encryption process or defining a specific security metric known as security amplitude. This paper explores the pros and cons of these approaches, demonstrating both efficient and insecure implementations of different suggestions along the way. Furthermore, we introduced two novel ways to implement uncloneable encryption using quantum computations and proved the feasibility of creating secure uncloneable encryption with relatively small key sizes.

This study proposes a novel, keyless authentication procedure for physical layers, specifically for Gaussian noise channels. Unlike conventional approaches that require an exchange of encrypted messages to verify identity, this method directly leverages the characteristics of these channels to determine device authenticity. The proposed system consists of a simple, real-time authentication module that, although not benefiting from the exchange of encrypted messages, offers enhanced security through a more complex cipher. The success of this system is demonstrated through simulations, showing that authentication accuracy surpasses 90% for a 10 kilobit-per-second data transfer rate. The code for this research is available online.

We utilized the full tight-binding model and random phase approximation to
explore flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer molybdenum disulfide.
Our calculations showed that lattice relaxation influences plasmon behavior.
When we considered intraband transitions, low-damped, flat plasmons emerged,
while accounting for interband transitions led to plasmon dispersion following
$\sqrt q$ law. The plasmon energies in these materials can be adjusted through
tweaking the twist angles and doping levels. For samples without lattice
relaxations, coexistence of low and high-energy plasmons occurs. Higher doping
levels however eliminate the quasi-flat plasmon. These observations imply that
two conditions must be satisfied: a flat band isolated from the other bands
and adequate doping level to witness the quasi-flat plasmon. The study offers
clues for exploring superconductivity mediated by plasmons in these materials.

This paper expresses the potential function $f$ associated with an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold in terms of the scalar field $p$, determining when the potential function is constant, and establishing a link between $f$ and $\lambda$. We also establish a condition for a conformal Ricci soliton to be a gradient Ricci soliton, and provide a characterization of the soliton in terms of its contraction or expansion rate.

Both celestial bodies can experience significant mass loss due to an expansive outward flow, which can be driven by numerous mechanisms including intense radiation, shock waves, and energy generated within the body. A powerful magnetic field can contain or even redirect this mass loss if it extends beyond the body's surface, interacting with the surrounding environment. The resulting interaction can create an magnetic field-controlled accumulation of material around the body, both if the mass loss is substantial, like in the case of massive stars, or minimal, like in the case of small planets. Although the underlying physics is similar for both, the characteristic features of these phenomena are influenced by the nature of the underlying body, its gravitational pull, and the resulting density and surface characteristics. As such, the distinctive patterns of an expanding wind, a swirling magnetosphere, and a surrounding envelope or atmosphere may differ significantly between a massive star and a small planet.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to a better comprehension of 3D topological materials. Proximity effect has been successfully achieved with experimental techniques like angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, but the theoretical description of these effects requires more development. In this study, the influence of interface interaction on the proximity effect has been examined using a ferromagnetic cobalt layer proximal to a bismuth surface. Our model highlights the significance of electron scattering at the interface and suggests that proximity effect models should account for interface interaction.

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Verification of results is achieved by comparison with existing works, particularly for $\alpha=1$. Numerical examples, including a diatomic molecule, demonstrate energy eigenvalue and bound state eigenfunction calculations.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimization problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularization. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets.

Sequential language models are highly versatile, consistently demonstrating success in various NLP tasks. One crucial aspect of these models is their ability to capture sentence-level structure. Although extensively tested for English, similar performance for other languages remains unexplored. We examine the potential of using an LSTM-based system for a morphologically complex language like Basque, with a focus on understanding whether it can recognize sentence concord (agreement). Our findings show that although the system is capable of recognizing concord to some extent, there are instances of severe error patterns. A key insight gained from this research is the need to consider sentence conjoinability, which provides a more comprehensive metric for evaluating a system's understanding of sentence structure and concord. Our analysis suggests that the inability of the system to learn certain instances of concord may be attributed to its inability to recognize sentence conjoinability. Moreover, his research highlights the importance of combining paradigm-based and lexicon-based approaches for accurately identifying a language's morphology.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 111-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon allow scientists to study this process, offering valuable insights into how planets with temperatures above 1500K lose heat. However, data from previous transit measurements are no longer accurate due to the planet's evolving orbit, at a rate of 4 seconds per year, which poses a challenge for scientists in predicting future transits accurately. As a result, there is a risk that scheduled observations for HD80606b with the JWST could be missed. To address this issue, researchers have conducted in-depth analyses of transit data from a global network of telescopes, utilizing the Delfi-C3 satellite, which provides high-precision measurements that are less susceptible to planetary system effects, allowing for a more accurate calculation of the planet's orbital path. By incorporating these findings, scientists aim to ensure that the scheduled observations for HD80606b with the JWST are as effective as possible, offering a chance to gain valuable insights into the planet's heat loss behavior.

Foundations games such as Chess, Bingo, and Tic-Tac-Toe have proven effective in introducing basic game concepts to newcomers. Research has also shown that adaptations of these games can be beneficial for individuals with neurological disorders such as Parkinson's disease and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). However, current applications of foundations games in neurorehabilitation lack a clear theoretical foundation and often focus solely on reports of anecdotal success. To better understand the underlying mechanics of foundations games and their potential to support rehabilitation, this study examines the cognitive processes involved in playing these games through a systematic design approach. By identifying the specific cognitive requirements for each game, researchers can prioritize specific goals for patients with specific cognitive abilities, thereby creating personalized assessments and modifying the games to tailor the challenges to the patients' capabilities. Through this approach, healthcare professionals can engage patients in meaningful activities that promote cognitive development and motivation, even when the patients are unable to complete the game as intended.

This research introduces an energy-based model that incorporates a variational approximation, allowing the representation of brittle phenomena through weak convergence techniques. The model includes a piecewise-rigid map field and a scalar field, both of which are utilized in a structured first-order functional that the pair must minimize. Key objectives include analyzing the convergence of the approximated model, characterizing the obtained functions in the limit case, and demonstrating numerical solutions using an implicit gradient scheme.

We investigate how a specific type of vector leptoquark that participates in third-generation weak interactions can produce Drell-Yan dilepton patterns, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. Our analysis considers various lepton-flavorscasing and mass differences, and for the first time, incorporates a precise calculation of QCD corrections to charge-boson and W-boson production in a complete framework, combining it with accurate parton shower simulations. Our findings serve as a foundation for thorough searches of this type of vector leptoquark in high-energy collisions, particularly in experiments that identify hadronically decayed electrons or muons.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings.

Personalization is ubiquitous in modern technology, improving user experience and efficiency. Yet, it can also compromise users' privacy in exchange for tailored recommendations. I argue that this trade-off is inherent to the concept of personalization. Based on the principles of normative privacy, I contend that users' willingness to sacrifice some privacy for personalization is rational. This willingness is driven by the principle of benefit maximization. In contrast, the aversion to personalization among those who value privacy highlights the importance of protecting individuals' autonomy and upholding the principle of privacy.

Previous linguistic analyses, as seen in the work of centering theory, highlight correlations between specific sentence structures and the development of anaphoric understanding. We argue that these patterns of association should be considered part of a shared cognitive framework, accessible to all individuals within a culture, including those whose native language is the corpus source. Furthermore, we propose that neural networks, when trained to resolve coreference, are learning to recognize and capitalize on this universal cognitive framework, independent of the specific language being modeled. Empirical evidence from various coreference resolution tasks across different languages is presented to support this proposition. When neural coreference models are evaluated using centering theory's scoring metric, our findings reveal that they exhibit a strong correlation with human judgments when compared to traditional evaluation metrics. Moreover, this scoring metric is particularly useful in identifying the aspects of these models that are truly coreference-related. When tested on multiple languages and coreference datasets, this knowledge remain remarkably stable. Additionally, we find that the performance of these models is largely dependent on the presence of certain linguistic features related to centering, and there is room for improvement in achieving human-like anaphoric understanding.

We have developed a set of parameters that collaborate to comprehensively identify all possible upward planar embeddings of a directed acyclic graph. Specifically, the parameters in question are related to the layout of the graph and are expressed in terms of an underlying set of drawings. We have successfully fragmented the vast Parameterized Upward Planarity class into more manageable subclasses for both fixed and variable embeddings, essentially solving the main problems associated with upward planar drawings. These problems include the recognition of double-conic surfaces, the creation of cone-triple free environments, and the determination of whether a graph can be represented as a triple-conic surface. Our comprehensive analysis also covers cone-triple free variable upward planar drawings, revealing the conditions under which such graphs can be rendered as triple-conic free variable upward planar drawings.

The growing intricacy of modern computer systems demands considerable time and expertise to set up correctly, slowing down development pace and causing difficulties for new users to enter the loop. To bridge this challenge, we propose a novel automated configuration technique for distributed reflection architectures, leveraging Artificial Intelligence to streamline setup processes. By recognizing optimal parameter combinations, our approach speeds up setup processes, eliminates tedious trial-and-error methods, and ensures reliable performance consistency. We showcase the effectiveness of this method through a practical application using a distributed kernel learning framework.

The average growth of a given set of operators in a quantum system is often assessed using the standard operator growth (SOG) framework. A distinct approach known as the mutual information growth (MIG) framework has also been proposed to analyze the operator growth phenomenon. In this study, we examine the MIG framework in relation to the SOG framework. We provide a universal bound for the growth of MIG in periodic quantum systems that follows a scaling law similar to that of the SOG. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both bounds on the SOG and MIG can be reached by models that exhibit efficient quantum chaos. Additionally, we find that in periodic quantum systems, the SOG and MIG overlap for a significant period of time, with both frameworks exhibiting distinct features in their early stages.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi access points and client devices need to be configured in a manner that enables accurate range estimation. Nevertheless, adjusting configuration parameters to achieve optimal results is a complex task.

This research centers on developing an innovative approach to predicting the distance between WiFi access points and client devices, utilizing a supervised machine learning model. Our analysis utilized 1500 data points collected in a university library, spanning a distance of 10 to 30 meters from each WiFi access point. Our goal was to create a solution that could accurately forecast the distance within a 1-meter margin, given the data collected does not cover the full 10-meter range some machines operate with.

Our data collection consisted of transmitting 5000 distinct WiFi packets from one location, resulting in the reception of these packets at a nearby site. This process was repeated across the entire 30-meter extent, allowing us to build a reliable range estimation model. Our analysis revealed that a combination of WiFi signal strength and round-trip time can predict the distance within a 1-meter margin. Furthermore, our findings indicate that using a large dataset may lead to machines operating with a wider range, potentially exceeding the actual distance by 5 meters.

We're taking an unconventional approach to address the cosmic dawn by utilizing massive black holes as the primary objects. These supermassive black holes formed early in the universe's development and resided at its center. We're investigating a novel scenario in which the early universe's stellar engines, failed to form compact objects, instead gave rise to massive shells that radiate energy through gravity. This scenario has the potential to explain the observed energy released during the cosmic dawn if it occurred in regions where the density of baryons is high. Using a simple model for radiative transfer, we found that a Dyson shell around a black hole with a mass similar to the Milky Way's can release ~10^11 times the energy emitted by the sun at a wavelength of 0.1 micron, for a duration of one billion years, if it orbits the black hole at a distance of 10 parsecs. This energy could have been observed from a distance of 100 megaparsecs, matching the findings of the Hubble Space Telescope. Furthermore, in this scenario, the shell's motion induces gravitational waves that may have been detected by LIGO's sensitivity, specifically in the region of the gravitational wave spectrum associated with the cosmic dawn. We propose that future observations with the James Webb Space Telescope and the Square Kilometre Array can be used to test this theory and its predictions.

Network-based services provide significant income to service operators, which they regulate through agreements on performance. Ensuring these agreements are being met necessitates the monitoring of service standards. A method to accomplish this involves deploying a system of active measurement nodes within the network. These nodes would be responsible for carrying out periodic checks on performance and notifying the operator if any standard is breached. However, maintaining an up-to-date list of measurable performance standards across the network poses a challenge. It is this problem that our proposed system aims to address using peer-to-peer technology.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Although the regenerative beam breakup instability is the most critical concern, there's a lack of clear guidelines due to the limited availability of detailed particle motion data. Our research demonstrates the significant impact of fill pattern on beam breakup frequency and growth rate by illustrating the effects in a 11.4 GeV fat-beam electron storage ring designed for Thomson Scattering Machines, both with a round and a long fill pattern. The particle motion data were generated using the PYCUDA implementation of the multi-particle macroparticle model, where each macroparticle comprises 10,000 particles to account for the high charge of fat beams. The results show that the beam breakup frequency remains relatively constant and is determined by the RF cavity, whereas the growth rate is influenced by the fill design and beam distribution at the start of each pass, highlighting the importance of careful beam injection and potential use of beam focusing techniques to enhance stability.

To determine resonance angles in neutron resonance spectroscopy, accurately measuring the total cross-section is crucial. Until now, measuring this cross-section has been challenging for complex materials like carbon. This study introduces a groundbreaking scintillator sensor using three-dimensional projection and convolutional neural networks for event identification, EnNeX-1. This sensor was tested by firing 3.2 GeV neutrons at various depths within a block composed of polyethylene and carbon, before observing the resulting signals. Unlike conventional approaches, EnNeX-1 bypasses the need for explicit function parameters, directly estimating the total cross-section based on signal characteristics. This led to a previously unachievable level of precision in measuring total cross-sections for complex materials like carbon.

In a previous series of experiments, we discovered how sticking forces changed in response to temperature among particles made of chondritic materials, which indicated that their surface energy drops by approximately 5 times when temperatures rise. In the present investigation, we shift focus to the effect of surface moisture on the grains under normal lab conditions, which involves having multiple water layers. In the case of the cooler protoplanetary discs and moderate temperatures, grains likely only hold one water layer. Since this water layer would evaporate in the warmer sections of the discs as dust moves inward, we decided to examine how two alternative methods for dust preparation affect tensile strength, which involved letting the grains dry in the air (resulting in dry samples) or baking them into airless environments (yielding super-dry samples) as an attempt to mimic how things might appear in the cooler sections of the protoplanetary discs. In all experiments where temperatures didn't exceed 1000 K, we discovered that dry samples displayed increased sticking by approximately 10 times over their water-soaked counterparts. In temperatures of up to 900 K, super-dry samples behave identically to dry samples. Nevertheless, sticking forces in the super-dry samples shoot up to yet another increase of about 100 times in temperatures of about 1200 K. These findings imply that aggregate growth accelerates in a narrow high-temperature range, which may be a critical'sweet spot' for planetary growth.

This R package, lfda, facilitates the implementation of local fisher discriminant analysis (LFDA) across various contexts. The LFDA method is an adaptive version of the traditional fisher discriminant analysis (FDA), tailored to process datasets with complex structures. The package enables users to execute both local and global variations of FDA, including KLFDA and VLFDA, as well as traditional FDA through the preprocessed LFDA framework. Furthermore, lfda offers a user-friendly interface for optimizing parameter values, visualizing model components, and performing sensitivity analysis to evaluate dimensionality reduction stability.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental factors, the Complex Action Observation Learning (CAOL) framework has been particularly successful in teaching robots to mimic observations even with complex nonlinear constraints and avoidable obstacles. However, most observed trajectories in real-world datasets are tailored to accommodate linear constraints, reflecting the limited efficacy of conventional methods in handling complex scenarios. To address this shortfall, this research introduces the Extended Complex Action Observation Learning (EKMP) framework to enable the efficient transfer of skills to tackle a broader range of nonlinear constraints, making it viable to learn from a wider range of data. In contrast to traditional optimization methods with linear constraints that rely on gradient-based optimisation, the EKMP framework harnesses the computational advantages of quadratic optimisation to speed up processing time, reducing the computational burden by half. The research is further bolstered by the successful execution of 1500 random setups on a real robotic platform and the openness of the code and dataset for use by the robotic community.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs.

A novel Rashba interaction that separates into two components, with opposite signs, is introduced in an attractive Hubbard model with spin-orbit coupling. It's demonstrated that this distinction may result in a quantum spin singlet state within the Rashba gap, which can be characterized by dual $su(2)$ spin rotation symmetries. The superfluid state represented by this model exhibits topological properties, specifically fractionalized fermion and boson modes in vortex states. The interplay between Rashba interaction, Rashba gap, and spin-orbit coupling can be explored through mean-field theory, revealing that the topological superfluid state may emerge across various Rashba gap sizes. Additionally, the interplay between Rashba interaction and spin-orbit coupling may lead to the stabilization of this topological state when the Rashba gap is negative. Direct evidence of the topological nature of this superfluid state is provided by the accumulation of density of states at the Rashba gap zero-crossing and in vortex states.

By utilizing scanning tunneling microscopy to analyze the surface structure of oxygen-doped Pb surfaces and comparing this to results from positron emission spectroscopy in Mg-doped $Al_2O_3$, we have observed the interplay between lattice disorder and type of correlation in $d$-orbitals in these materials.  The findings indicate that in $d$-orbital space, a two-dimensional vortex lattice transforms into a vortex solid filled with the arrangement of correlated squares when the type of correlation changes from isosceles to right-angled angles.  This transition to correlated vortex binding is seen to occur near the critical dose of $d$-type scattering and may provide a more stable path for superconductivity in the mixed state.  The change in vortex lattice structure is identifiable by the release of condensed Cooper pairs as the type of correlation transforms from isosceles to angular, resulting in the emission of positrons at an energy of ${\sim}0.12$ eV, which is the energy of the zero-binding-energy pair.  The type of correlation is found to be influenced by the movement of ions in the material and can be controlled through the concentration of dopants, enabling the selection of the vortex lattice structure and providing a way to manage the type of correlation in $d$-orbital space.  This discovery may provide a path for optimizing the performance of correlated materials and may also offer a way to understand other phenomena that arise due to the transition of

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a new class of models, incorporating a distinct 'exclusion zone' region. Nonetheless, the geometry of this exclusion area remains unclear, especially at low surface curvatures. A novel approach has been introduced in this study to investigate the geometry of the exclusion area in detail. By combining the 'weak-stretch' scenario with the'strong-stretch' scenario under low surface curvatures, the analysis reveals that the exclusion area takes on a triangular shape near the grafting interface, with this geometry remaining unchanged regardless of the brush's elongation. This finding is attributed to the prevalent angle of approximately 90 degrees between nearby polymer chains. The area's triangular shape has significant implications for brush thickness and density. The theoretical framework also offers practical guidelines for predicting triangular cross-sectional dimensions in the wake of surface curvature changes.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A minimal identifying set exists and its smallest size is known as the metric dimension of the graph. Here we discuss the concept of the trimmed metric dimension, which represents the smallest size of a set that identifies the graph after removing a specified number of points.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image analysis, applying it to all-sky maps created from Fermi-LAT data. The primary objective was to modify the standard map-making procedure to retain more detailed spatial information, making sources with variable patterns more discernible. The study compared machine learning-based image enhancement, involving U-Net and Generative Adversarial Networks, to the established method. The findings showed these models successfully extracted latent representations of gamma-ray skies, revealing new sources and enhancing detection of known variables with radiation patterns that change over time. The study also demonstrated how these models can be trained on limited data, incorporating additional information from other observational frequencies, and successfully identified key sources with variable radiation patterns that match established lists.

A serial majority graph represents a collection of binary preferences, where a voter's preferences are a sequential path due to at least two distinct restrictions being applied. These restrictions stipulates that adjacent preferences must be opposite in orientation and that no voter's most preferred alternative is second-least preferred. This paper focuses on identifying an equilibrium where no voter's opinion inferences are disputed. It proves that finding an equilibrium in a serial majority network is computationally complex, but this difficulty is overcome by providing a specific algorithm that reaches an equilibrium in a serial majority network. This same algorithm is then applied to demonstrate computational complexity in scenarios where key properties of serial majority networks are manipulated.

We conducted a comprehensive search for binary asters, also known as Mizar stars, within the Pan-STARRS1 point source catalog. These influential stars have a noticeable effect on the motion of nearby O-type stars, particularly high-mass X-ray binaries. The detection of binary asters is crucial in studying the origin of pulsar velocities as well as the formation mechanisms of binary systems containing high-mass X-ray binaries. By considering the possible range of distances to these stars, we performed a stratified analysis of their potential presence. Our findings suggest that binary asters should be abundant enough to account for the observed pulsar velocity distributions when considering a wide range of angles, however, their actual velocity spread is underlined by pulsar bias in statistical samples. Additionally, we discovered potential candidates for binary asters, which if confirmed, could explain the velocity distributions reported in previous studies.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper's first section explores the asymptotic behavior of the estimators presented in section 2 of the Auerbach's work. The second section investigates extensions to the model. The third section applies the model to estimate peer influence effects within networks. The fourth section presents results obtained from simulated data.

This research paper introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives a new type of the Leibniz Rule by modifying the standard formula, and establishes this modified version as equivalent to another form that can be expressed with the use of the Euler formula. Additionally, the paper presents specific cases of this new rule, including applications to variable-order fractional powers and combinations of variable-order fractional derivatives.

This paper investigates how complex signals are detected using complex data that varies spatially. We develop a general statistical model that measures the performance of discrete Fourier transform-based detectors and derive optimal techniques, such as maximum likelihood estimation, by minimizing this measure. We also examine the limitations of these techniques and explore ways to apply this research to areas like communication system multi-antenna technology and medical imaging.

We've developed an open-source suite of web tools to streamline the processing of imaging and spectral data for multi-band observations. These tools are designed to automate tasks associated with combining data from various facilities, such as space-based missions like PanSTARRS, Gaia, and SIMBD, as well as ground-based observations with APOGEES, KEPLER, and others. By utilizing JavaScript and cross-domain request technologies, the suite enables seamless integration of data from diverse sources, enabling rapid computation of quantities like distances, luminosities, and temperature parameters for individual stars and celestial objects. The platform also facilitates extensive data visualization, including plots of luminosity versus temperature, Hertzsprung-Russell diagrams, phase diagrams, and spectral displays using Aladin. Furthermore, the suite enables the creation of custom plots, spectral displays, and maps of the sky, among other visualizations. Additionally, the platform is complemented by a comprehensive documentation site, providing access to user guides, tutorials, and a frequently asked questions section.

The Southern Atlantic rift underwent a significant change in opening direction and rate over time, influencing the development of adjacent margin geometry. To better understand this complex process, researchers analyzed multiple datasets, including magnetic anomalies, seaward-dipping reflectors, and margin kinematics. By dividing the rift into five distinct regions and considering various time periods, they reconstructed opening displacement and azimuth. In the northwest, the rift exhibited rapid early extension with a nearly E-W direction, later changing to a more SE-Directed opening in the late stages. In the central area, the rift showed a mixed record with varying opening directions and rates. In the northeast, early extension was characterized by a SE-Directed opening with increased rates in the late stages. Models of stratigraphic patterns and crustal accretionary arrays were also applied to each region, providing additional insights into mantle flow and deformation processes.

A proven strategy to enhance segmentation models through unsupervised training is information maximization, but care must be taken when labeling boundaries as they are often poorly defined and highly variable. To tackle this issue, we propose a new unsupervised unsupervised training method for segmentation based on preserving valuable information from uncertain boundary regions. This approach involves two main components: first, we create a semantic map through an unsupervised unsupervised training of a encoder; second, we implement a custom loss function to focus on optimizing uncertain boundary regions. We utilized this method on the segmentation of cardiac left ventricles from MRI images. It achieved competitive results on two public benchmark datasets, according to evaluation metrics including dice similarity coefficient and mean Hausdorff distance. Furthermore, it demonstrated robustness in handling noisy data and a notable reduction in boundary variability.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context.

Similar to other research fields, machine learning also benefits from utilizing a broad range of data.  However, utilizing a broad range of data can be challenging due to the existence of diverse languages in many applications, such as online content or dictionaries.  One machine learning task that is particularly affected by such diversity is supervised word sense differentiation.  In contrast to other tasks like word classification or translation that can rely on existing annotations, word sense differentiation necessarily involves existing annotations on a word-by-word basis.  Existing methods for word sense differentiation typically employ embedded representations of words that are derived from large-scale language data and apply statistical techniques to identify sense-specific distributions.  Unlike other applications of such methods, the performance of which is largely determined by the quality of the word representations, the outcome also depends significantly on the degree of lexical semantic variation in the learning data.  To address this issue, we propose a new approach that is designed to discover latent variation in lexical meanings during the word sense differentiation process.  In particular, our approach is centered around the idea that words with embedded representations that exhibit significant differences during the differentiation process may indicate the presence of multiple senses, whereas words with similar distributions do not.  To implement this idea, we developed a new technique that learns word sense-specific distributions by identifying embedded representations of words that are distinct from the overall distribution of words.  To evaluate this approach, we discovered that it is capable of matching or outperforming existing methods for the English language and significantly improving the performance of

We propose a new approach to understanding the distribution of quarks and gluons in momentum space, based on an established principle from statistical mechanics. By utilizing a function that depends on the relative momentum between particles, we derive a detailed formula that incorporates this dependence. This results in a complex distribution function with multiple components, affecting both the quark and gluon distributions. Specifically, it leads to an increased distribution of particles with high relative momenta, which aligns with the principles of the Higgs mechanism. Additionally, we show that the new function leads to the emergence of chiral condensates in massless QCD, and that it differentiates between the distribution of quark and antiquark flavors. Further, we find that the new function causes the mass of the $f_0$ meson to arise dynamically, and that it results in the polarization of the vacuum, giving rise to particles in pairs.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area of ongoing biophysical investigation. Research indicates that knots integral to a protein's native structure may play a significant role in its binding affinity, resistance to degradation, and overall function. However, uncovering the underlying relationship between protein knots and folding is a challenging task due to the large dimensionality of a protein's conformational space. In our study, we introduce a novel approach to evaluating the topology of protein structures based on their oscillatory patterns, which allows us to assess the integrity of spatial filaments in these proteins. By applying this approach to a diverse set of linearly knotted proteins, we identify a distinct topological signal characteristic of banded knotted structures and, for the first time, visually demonstrate various knotted proteins' potential binding pathways. Our method demonstrates the potential to tackle complex problems at the intersection of biophysics and topology, and the accompanying software is available online for users to explore binding pathways in knotted proteins.

To address the Hubble tension, some researchers have suggested the existence of early dark energy (EDE). Although this theory is appealing, its parameters must be narrowly defined in order to resolve the tension. Utilizing the Planck and BOSS datasets through a profile likelihood method, we have constrained the EDE parameters and found that the amplitude of the EDE density must be below 0.037 at a 68% confidence level. This finding holds when considering a model that includes matter-scattering, and Scarpino-Sfondrato et al.'s cosmological constants model is also examined.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite.

A detailed examination of the Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem is performed, 
focusing on an unusual, not-obviously-trivial aspect to clarify its 
understanding. Initial steps involve reviewing the conditions for the NG
theorem's validity, then exploring alternative, equivalent conditions.
Subsequently, the theorem's application and implications are examined
through specific examples, including both relativistic and nonrelativistic
theories, to demonstrate its robustness and universal applicability.
Finally, the relationship between the NG theorem and other physical principles
is discussed, addressing potential misconceptions and misconstructions of the
theorem's requirements.

Recent advances in large language models have highlighted their capability to model complex language structures and engage in social conversations. These models can also be trained on theoretical language data, simulating the language generation aspects of multiple formal systems. In this research, we explore the possibility of reducing the computational complexity of these models when generating abstract sentence patterns, particularly in ontological axioms. We demonstrate that through a combination of expert guidance and continuous evaluation, these models can efficiently produce more accurate and varied sentence patterns. Furthermore, our findings indicate that these models can strike a balance between generating practical real-world sentences and abstract sentence patterns, even when applied to complex domains. We showcase the effectiveness of this approach through multiple systems generated through this method, and our results suggest that they outperform multiple existing machine learning models and even approach the performance of professionally crafted examples.

In this study, we determined the total chromatic numbers along with their equitable and neighborhood sum distinguishing counterparts for specific types of circulant graphs. Our findings apply to the integers 2 and 3 when the circulant graph satisfies particular degree and connection criteria. Additionally, our results include the computation of total chromatic numbers for certain types of circulant graphs on 12 vertices.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This research offers a novel perspective on the equilibrium among remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy through the case of a particular Heusler compound, L1_0 FePt. By integrating analytical techniques and transmission electron microscopy, it's discovered that remote and pinhole epitaxy coexist and prevail in areas distant from holes, whereas the Heusler compound tends towards van der Waals epitaxy within these holes. A theoretical model explains the prevalence of remote and pinhole epitaxy by referencing the energy associated with misfit dislocations, which is minimized when the distance between them exceeds 100 nm, a value consistent with the size of the hexagonal graphene domain. It's also found that applying a 2 MeV ion beam accelerates the transition to remote and pinhole epitaxy, likely by displacing contaminants and organizing the Fe and Pt rows across the interface. This breakthrough enables the production of defect-free L1_0 FePt films through remote epitaxy, featuring exceptional magnetic properties, and offers insights that can be applied to other Heusler compounds.

This paper delves into the study of $p$-ary $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes, initially presented in a previous work where their rank and distance properties were examined. Here, we further investigate their dimension and erosional characteristics for all possible code parameters within the scope of $p$-ary $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes.

The production of secondary hydrocarbons through injection of a polymer solution in porous media is modeled, with the goal of maximizing long-term daily production rates. By leveraging the concept of an optimal control structure in finite horizon cases, the problem is formulated as a variant of the linear quadratic optimal control problem. The solution involves two main components: first, the establishment of a state transition matrix; second, the derivation of a feedback control law. This feedback law is expressed in a Riccati equation form, considering the finite horizon context. Furthermore, a specific focus is placed on characterizing the polymer plugs injection profiles that maximize production rates.

When dealing with high-dimensional data and complex classifications, it is common to encounter situations where a positive sample cannot be classified independently. In such cases, utilizing additional information from negative examples associated with the same label can be beneficial. However, when working with large datasets, accessing a comprehensive set of negative examples for each possible class becomes impractical. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed several methods to partner positive samples with a limited number of labeled examples for each class. These methods typically focus on utilizing nearby unsampled regions of the data space that are not represented by positive examples, as they are likely to contain negative examples. Given a positive sample and the corresponding class, the goal is to identify a suitable region R in the data space that accurately predicts class C over area S. Existing approaches either rely on specific types of models or incorporate additional information that is not directly related to the data. In our work, we propose a suitable region R that minimizes the risk of predicting the wrong class over the entire data space S, without relying on specific models or additional information. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by conducting rigorous experiments on real-world datasets, and it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods using strong baselines.

This study investigates the energy bound of the modified Allen-Cahn equation with a time-fractional term, specifically focusing on the upper bound as the diffusion parameter diminishes. Existing research typically assumes the initial data has zero mean, but this analysis relaxes that restriction, instead establishing a relationship between the energy bound and the time derivative of the phase-field function. A key finding emerges when $\epsilon$ is very small, revealing that the energy bound may decrease over time and can even become nonpositive, despite appearing physically unsustainable. However, this discrepancy can be resolved by introducing an extra term representing the capacity of the spatial domain, thereby ensuring the energy bound always remains nonnegative.

The relationship between physical states and observable quantities is governed by the principle of positivistic efficacy, which can be represented as a bijective correspondence between certain categories. This correspondence induces a categorical representation of physical states as equivalence classes of observables, and vice versa. The same principle also establishes a categorical equivalence between the category of physical states and the category of observable quantities. This equivalence can be realized through a 2-categorical connection, which provides the framework for formulating the physical requirements in terms of categorical and functorial conditions. The positivity efficacy principle can be applied to formulate the requirements for a physical theory with a given set of observable quantities, and this is illustrated using the example of a free boson field.

The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from particles interacting with disk matter or a surrounding magnetic field could provide a potential explanation.  To better comprehend this, we analyzed the properties of a nearby galaxy (IC 1101) using data from the Fermi and MAGIC telescopes.  By examining how gamma-rays are affected by energy and observation time, we determined that radiation is likely a result of hadronic radiation from particles interacting with a surrounding magnetic field, rather than the space around a black hole.  This could be confirmed by searching for signs of how gamma-rays affect the magnetic field's ability to absorb particles.  Additionally, managing the belief that hadronic radiation comes from a specific mechanism involves updating a statistical analysis tool using a particular dataset.  This could provide more clear evidence for a particular theory.

This research investigates how portfolio returns are allocated across different stock categories and suggests developing a new method that leverages machine learning to classify stocks directly from price data. We demonstrate this approach using a large dataset of UK stocks and showcase its effectiveness by predicting future portfolio returns and identifying undervalued stocks. The method's success suggests that a more efficient portfolio can be created using stock classifications based on natural language processing techniques.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate sound recordings are compromised by background noise and the inherent distortion of traditional stethoscopes, making it essential to develop noise-resistant methods for heart sound analysis.  This study recorded heart sounds under various conditions using both digital and stethoscope recordings, with added Gaussian and white noise as well as distortion from two different stethoscopes.  Our research involved training a convolutional neural network using a dataset of cardiac sounds with added Gaussian and white noise as well as distortion from one type of stethoscope.  This network demonstrated high accuracy even with extremely loud background noises and significant frequency distortions, suggesting that deep learning algorithms like this one have a high potential for real-world cardiac sound analysis.  This potential was further confirmed by testing the network with sounds recorded using the second type of stethoscope, indicating that a single training session can yield a versatile model capable of accurately identifying cardiac sounds with significantly different sound profiles.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare. FedHealth aggregates data via a federated approach, leveraging transfer learning to develop personalized models for each user. The framework comprises two main components. Initially, a federated dataset is created through wearables via a data collection module. Secondly, a federated transfer learning module builds personalized models for each user. We demonstrate the efficacy of FedHealth by developing two practical applications - activity recognition and sleep stage classification. Comparison with existing models confirms the superiority of FedHealth in terms of accuracy. Furthermore, we examine the scalability of FedHealth through a modular approach, showcasing the framework's potential for broad healthcare applications.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations.

In string compactifications, we suggest that dark energy marks the universe's end, 
potentially triggered by decompactification, addressing the cosmological coincidence issue. 
Lack of stable de Sitter vacua forces us to model dark energy as a slow-rolling quintessence field. 
This process inevitably leads to a chaotic, universe-altering phase shift, likely after several hundred 
cosmological time cycles. Dark energy dominance, therefore, cannot persist forever, and the chance 
exists that we reside in the universe's first epoch. Our quintessence model illustrates the 
dysfunctional universe dynamics resulting from the descent of heavy states, when a multitude of particles 
are produced, overshadowing the quintessence's power. Additionally, our theory raises implications 
for the universe's early inflationary periods.

The rapid evolution of software applications is forcing vendors to rely heavily on user-generated content for guidance, which in turn is being provided through documentation and online forums. While these sources are invaluable, they are typically plagued by a lack of structured organization, making it impossible for traditional question-answering systems to effectively utilize them. In response, there is a growing need for more advanced methods of automated software processing, which can handle real-world complexity and mix of structural and unorganized content. This article defines a new approach and framework for achieving this goal, outlines the technical details of a working implementation, and presents early results from both narrow and broad applications of the technology.

This study tackles a complex control problem where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in response to specific threshold levels. The analysis assumes that these sudden changes are part of a process that follows a random walk. Despite the costs being able to change suddenly, the optimal control strategy remains a continuous function of the current state. The research demonstrates that the optimal approach can be represented as the expected value of the best response to a given scenario, taking into account all possible outcomes of the random walk that influence the costs. This is achieved by establishing a new comparison principle that relates the optimal approach to a specific class of dynamic programming problems.

To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates unequal leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and aid in identifying its potential. Unequal production, where one leptoquark has a higher momentum than the other, is analyzed in various contexts, including both scalar and vector leptoquark configurations. Our study establishes a comprehensive and efficient framework for computing relevant differential distributions and cross-sections, applying a set of consistent unitarity, renormalizability, and flavor principles. To accurately assess the effectiveness of this process in discovering leptoquark, our model is scrutinized using a realistic Monte Carlo simulation, considering all major contributions to unequal leptoquark creation in the Large Hadron Collider. Our findings will be presented in the form of meaningful constraints on leptoquark parameters, taking into account all available data from the Large Hadron Collider, including data from two separate energy levels.

This work focuses on guided learning of temporal sequences through limited and high-dimensional measurements, with applications in life science observations. We've developed a new model that utilizes a low-rank factorization to represent the temporal manifold, keeping the number of required measurements minimal. This model ensures coherent data representation, making it suitable for analysis and inference. We've also established an efficient algorithm to estimate the factorization, along with associated statistics. Specifically, we've derived an estimator for the low-rank structure and a coherent representation, along with corresponding asymptotic properties. We've conducted a numerical study to demonstrate the algorithm's performance and reliability. Finally, we've explored examples of guided learning in the context of life science observations, highlighting the benefits of our approach over existing methods.

We analyze the CIA (continuum induced absorption) lines of chlorine, which are under-stimulated due to low gas temperatures in the molecular disks of galaxies, affecting their absorption at 1.53 $\mu$m. By examining 21 cm line data for 16 galaxies and far-infrared data for 11 galaxies, we investigate the relationship between CIA absorption and various gas parameters. Our results show that CIA absorption is correlated with the excess radiation exiting the system's optical depth, and this excess is caused by under-stimulated coherent emission from chlorine atoms. We find that chlorine's emission is related to the system's total gas density and is maximized in systems with moderate density. However, extremely dense systems experience scattering that reverses the expected absorption pattern. We also discover a variety of gas regimes based on the relationship between CIA absorption and other gas parameters, and we find that CIA absorption can serve as an indicator of gas density in remote galaxies.

We address the anomalies recently reported in $K$ and $B$ meson decays, specifically involving the processes $K^+	o \pi^0 e^+ 
u_e$, $K^+	o \gamma e^+ 
u_e$, $B^0	o K^0 \epsilon^+ 
u_e$, and $B^0	o \gamma \epsilon^+ 
u_e$. We propose a comprehensive framework to simultaneously explain the deviations seen in these four processes. The key element of our framework is the introduction of a single heavy vector boson, $X$, with a mass of around 1 TeV, which originates from a vectorlike doublet. This boson contributes to the anomalous interactions in a way that involves the Higgs boson. As a result of this coupling, the Higgs boson's effective mass becomes around 100 MeV, which in turn affects the energy spectrum of the electron in the final state. We derive the explicit form of the form factors governing the electron's energy dependence. We also provide the theoretical predictions for the branching ratios and energy spectra in the mentioned processes, and our results match the experimental findings. Moreover, we derive the existing and future experimental and theoretical limits on the parameter space of our model, specifically on the mass of the vector boson and the Higgs boson's contribution.

Levenshtein initially explored the sequence reconstruction problem using Hamming distance as the metric. This problem was later extended to permutations in 2000 by Koivisto and Torkkola. Their work on the subject raised a sequence reconstruction problem involving arithmetical sequences, specifically focusing on permutations of the set {1, 2,..., n}. It is demonstrated in this paper that when n is a prime number, the only irreducible sequences under Hamming distance as the metric are the elementary arithmetical sequences with a common difference of 1. This conclusion is achieved through an proof of a more general theorem and its corollary. The general theorem seeks to identify the unique sequences that can be reconstructed from partial information using Hamming distance as the metric for arithmetical sequences with a common difference of d. The proof of this theorem relies on the application of a theorem related to the uniqueness of factorization in the integers and a key observation related to the cyclic nature of these sequences.

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand its scope, using a limited amount of data for each family and then relying on a more extensive range of examples to train a parent node. We achieved this by dividing instruments into strings, woodwind, brass, and keyboard categories, then employed a multi-layer Perceptron to determine the most likely family and instrument by exploring different approaches to using parent node information and conducting experiments to validate our method's effectiveness.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek answers to several questions but typically ask few if any questions directly. Our proposed dataset, named QAnch, is unique in categorizing questions that are commonly asked when reading academic papers. It comprises 10,000 question-answer pairs from multiple sources, where each question is linked to a specific section of a research paper. Our research indicates that current knowledge-base models perform worse compared to general-purpose models when answering QAnch questions. This knowledge-gap is attributed to the limited information provided in research paper citations, which are usually focused on supporting the underlying arguments. Nevertheless, we believe that enhancing the performance of these models will result in better overall understanding of the content within research papers.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for the PTA parameter space of interest. Furthermore, we introduce an improved approach using spline interpolation to enhance the computation speed for specific narrow-band PTA datasets. The implementation of these findings in the GWecc package enables seamless access to searching for such eccentric signals within PTA datasets via the ENTERPRISE platform.

We establish that in ASEP, a velocity process evolves according to a specific rule depending on the initial data, and this velocity process is connected to TASEP. Additionally, we prove that in a finite velocity process, there is a steady-state velocity distribution, and this steady-state can be represented as a system of equations derived from the TASEP queue. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in a finite ASEP system with block initial conditions, the velocity process can be interpreted as a TASEP system with a variable capacity site.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control.

We examine a Majorana fermion scenario using a Majorana fermion tunneling between two sites, and investigate its behavior as a fermionic fermion first-order mean-field theory is applied. This analysis reveals an anomalous "fermionic" behavior for the Majorana fermion in question, which is contrary to traditional expectations. It appears that this unusual behavior is a result of the Majorana fermion's ability to be represented by a real instead of a complex wavefunction. This representation allows for the application of a mathematical transformation, which leads to the Majorana fermion displaying an integer spin value. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the application of a p-type tunneling momentum space, rather than the traditionally used s-type, leads to the Majorana fermion displaying unusual mass and energy characteristics. This, in turn, results in the Majorana fermion's stability being ensured by an applied linear potential instead of the traditional type.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This platform can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the project's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent photoassociation, specifically focusing on its application to creating stable, spin-polarized atom-molecule pairs from already spin-polarized atoms. Our model represents the interplay between photoassociation and two-body collisions and considers various collisional processes, either coherent or incoherent, influenced by an additional laser. This framework also encompasses situations where two independent coherent processes occur. Our findings reveal that, in the presence of coherent collisions, a single laser can induce the conversion of two atoms into an atom-molecule pair, also leading to emittable coherent two-photon states. Furthermore, this model facilitates the design of experiments to investigate coherent collisional processes and the creation of superposition states in atom-molecule pairs.

Our proposed DNA-storage support structure provides efficient support for both data organization and update operations through a hierarchical system, leveraging Garvey-Quahtani codes to effectively handle errors commonly found in DNA data. This support system helps alleviate the performance limitations of previous approaches, particularly in supporting data updates and a hierarchical structure, while also incorporating a new decoding algorithm to handle the residual errors often encountered in DNA storage.

Topological phases of matter are distinguished by the unique properties of their momentum-space energy spectra. This particular feature, nodal lines, represents a reduced dimensionality of topological phenomenon, where singularities occur along lines rather than points. Research has been enhanced by computational models, but it has now reached the experimental stage with artificial photonic systems and other setups. Recent examples include fabricated materials with nodal lines in momentum space, allowing topological properties such as fermion-like behavior of light and protected winding lines without gaps.

A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention directed network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.
