Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered images, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up scene rendering. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently train deep models from synthetic images under realistic lighting conditions. We apply our approach to abductive inference in the presence of semi-transparent liquids and foils in images, demonstrating its advantage over optimization-based methods and models trained using bit-manipulation-based multi-view images, particularly in complex scenarios with various transparent layers. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhkpv/vss.

An emerging challenge in video analysis is presented by interlaced video, which is still widely used in various applications such as surveillance cameras and historical film preservation. The traditional post-processing re-scanning method used for these videos is both time-consuming and ineffective in maintaining original video quality. Another issue arises from the fact that many modern video analysis techniques are designed with progressive-scan video in mind, making them incompatible with interlaced video. Current attempts at restoring interlaced video through computational methods have not successfully replicated the optimal results achieved by the conventional re-scanning technique in terms of visual quality. This is because conventional methods involve a depth-based approach that involves a motion estimation component, which is not addressed by these attempts. A novel technique for interlaced video restoration is presented, leveraging deep learning to simultaneously estimate motion and interlacing. This technique is designed to be both real-time and adaptable to various video formats. The technique's effectiveness is demonstrated through various experimental results, showing significant quality improvements over existing methods in terms of both subjective and objective quality metrics.

The investigation revealed a disparity of approximately 0.1 fm in the root mean square radius of the neutron density distribution between non-relativistic mean field models and their relativistic counterparts. Further analysis revealed the discrepancy arises due to varying product values of the effective mass and one-body potential strength within the respective frameworks, with those values being governed by the Hugenholtz-Van Hove theorem. In contrast, the thickness of the neutron skin was found not to solely correlate with the symmetry potential but rather was heavily dependent on the nucleon effective mass.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the shallow water equations are simplified to a linear partial differential equation that can be solved explicitly, using a novel deep learning-based method known as the Functional Graph Attention Network. This solution is then combined with observations from river flow velocity sensors to train a model capable of predicting velocities rapidly and accurately. In our experiments, we demonstrate that this approach can estimate velocities within 0.15 meters per second of the actual value using existing data from the River Thames, and significantly outperforms traditional methods in terms of speed.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels.
This technique is appealingly simple, yet challenging to execute well, especially when using smartphones, which have limited manual control over exposure settings.
This study proposes an innovative approach to automatically select optimal exposure settings for smartphone HDR, which involves using a method called featureless filter selection.
This method leverages filter images, which are readily available on smartphones and can serve as surrogate sources for selecting optimal exposure settings.
The proposed approach includes two main components: first, a novel way to quantify scene brightness based on a reference image, which eliminates the need for calculating complex image histograms; second, an innovative fusion algorithm called weighted average filtering, which produces high-quality HDR images.
The proposed algorithm was tested using a smartphone app and compared to established techniques for HDR fusion, which involved 50 participants and used 200 randomly selected pairs of underexposed and overexposed images.
The results showed that the proposed algorithm outperformed all comparison methods, which was confirmed by repeated ANOVA tests.

In our proposed framework, we integrate the principles of causal learning into the latest advancements in deep learning methods. Causal learning is a well-established approach in machine learning that has been shown to provide more accurate and generalizable results, however it has not been fully incorporated into the latest deep learning techniques. Our goal is to address this limitation and provide a comprehensive overview of causal learning in machine learning. This will involve discussing the concepts of latent variables, directed acyclic graphs, and causal mechanisms, as well as more advanced topics such as causal deep learning for sequential data, multi-task learning, and robustness. Through a combination of theoretical background and practical applications, we aim to create a cohesive guide for researchers on the causal learning framework.

Achieving uniform and efficient gas-to-catalyst heat transfer in fixed bed reactors is crucial for overall process efficiency.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings within this environment has been a challenge until now.  Our research utilizes the unique capabilities of rapid magnetic resonance imaging to spatially and temporally map the temperature arrangements present in fixed beds in real-time.  By utilizing this approach, our study provides visual and quantitative evidence of the Arrhenius correlation frequently used to model particle spacing effects on heat transfer rates.  Furthermore, our results highlight the significance of arranging particles in a specific manner to optimize heat transfer performance.  Our novel temperature mapping method paves the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics at play in complex systems through direct observation of temperature arrangements, allowing for improvements to be made to the performance of reactors.

This note presents a proof for a specific case of the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which is based on the $b$-principle and the properties of a family of subfolds within a manifold of dimension one. The proof involves establishing the relationship between a certain morphism that preserves subfolds and a product of circles, to the category of oriented subfolds within a torus of dimension two. The basis of the proof lies in an inductive approach that utilizes the properties of a family of subfolds within a manifold of increasing complexity, to ultimately demonstrate the applicability of the $b$-principle.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation.

Research on random matrices with autonomous entries typically requires a specific condition that involves the combinatorial concept of non-crossing partitions. This paper explores what happens when this condition is removed in models that include sum-of-squares, the real eigenvalue property, and the interlacing property of non-increasing row sums. The result shows that adding another row essentially returns to a state similar to not removing any rows. The model with row sums constraints was previously an open problem. The methods used mix new techniques with old approaches that involved quasi-hermitian matrices, the combinatorial interpretation of the real eigenvalue property, and the sum-of-squares representation.

Persuasive promotional videos are becoming increasingly influential in shaping consumer behavior and promoting social causes through various mediums such as e-commerce platforms and non-profit initiatives. Given the time-consuming and resource-intensive process of producing such high-quality videos by professional teams, the field of AI-powered video creation has gained momentum. This field is unique due to its interdisciplinary nature, which presents a significant hurdle for researchers who are new to the subject. A current void exists in comprehensive surveys on AI-powered video creation, which is an area we aim to address through a thorough review of applicable AI techniques and the development of a taxonomy that breaks down the process into three distinct phases. This taxonomy includes visual material extraction, storyline development, and post-production enhancements to optimize viewing experience. We will also discuss the most commonly employed evaluation metrics, associated datasets, and the advantages and limitations of existing approaches within this field, while exploring promising areas for future research and development.

A critical factor in designing effective threat protection systems lies in their ability to successfully handle attacks that exploit vulnerabilities. Yet, a significant challenge arises from the intricate relationship between attackers and system protectors, particularly when both parties possess identical capabilities. This research addresses this challenge by introducing a novel metric, called "security efficacy," which is a relative measure of a system's protection effectiveness. We demonstrate the utility of this metric through its application to two notable examples – software diversity and virus detection systems. Furthermore, we investigate the implications of security efficacy on the behavior of self-aware systems capable of modifying their own components.

Recently, highly complex photonic structures are being fabricated for reduced loss and localized light manipulation, particularly in ultra-high frequency ranges. However, direct applications of photonic systems in THz spectroscopy and sensing are impeded by material losses. To overcome this challenge, this research introduces a novel approach using microacoustic metagratings fabricated via two-photon lithography, which can operate at these high frequencies despite material losses. These microacoustic structures, with sub-wavelength features, are designed to selectively filter negative incident waves and protect desired positive waves from interference. Both numerical simulations and experimental measurements validate our approach, with the potential to be expanded to lower frequency ranges, paving the way for widespread use in THz spectroscopy and sensing applications.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between modes in optical resonators and waveguides. The framework is highly versatile, allowing it to address various applications including photonic crystal structures, nanograin suspensions, and conventional waveguides. Key principles, such as reciprocity, conservation of energy and momentum, and the Poincaré lemma, are leveraged to derive a comprehensive set of equations. These equations can describe both linear and nonlinear phenomena, including dispersion, absorption, scattering, bi-algebraic scattering, four-wave mixing, and associated phase matching conditions. The framework is then applied to analyze a nanowire photonic crystal structure, revealing new insights into the interplay between linear and nonlinear effects.

This paper builds upon established connections between global asymptotic stability, bumpless transfer, and universal stabilization in regulation systems that can be controlled without bounds, also making converse theorems possible for specific classes of these systems.

A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed, high-resolution images from low-resolution ones, tested on turbulent flow at different Reynolds numbers. A comparative analysis of two convolutional neural network models was conducted to determine their effectiveness and efficiency in enhancing resolution without prior knowledge of flow characteristics. The research demonstrated that a straightforward GAN model can significantly improve resolution by at least 4-5 times with little loss of accuracy, surpassing traditional super-resolution techniques. It was further found that increasing Reynolds numbers above 4000 has an insignificant impact on flow characteristics.

The paper addresses the ambiguity in the scattering phase shift formula derived from quantum mechanics. It argues that the standard wave formula result emerges naturally if one accepts the principle that a partial wave behaves like a whole number of independent harmonic oscillators when the energy is sufficiently high. Additionally, it shows that this principle is logically compatible with the properties of plane waves and that it leads to the expected Born cross-section in the high-energy limit. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that this approach allows for the interpretation of phase shifts in terms of the formation of bound states or the creation of particles from the vacuum in quantum fluctuations.

The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural networks often struggle with this requirement due to their lack of intrinsic uncertainty representation. To address this issue, researchers have proposed various methods to manage uncertainty, categorizing them into three types: likelihood-based, penalty-based, and energy-based approaches. This study focuses on the open-world scenario, characterized by an infinite number of possible classes, and aims to develop an energy-based uncertainty model that can be learned in an end-to-end training process. Unlike previous methods, this model does not require prior assumptions about the data's characteristics or the network's uncertainty properties. Instead, it utilizes an explicitly designed energy function to represent uncertainty, which is learned through a contrastive training process. The proposed model's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to a specific use case, involving the recognition of celestial objects, where it achieves superior performance compared to multiple baseline uncertainty quantification methods.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies.

Understanding business processes relies heavily on process mining, which can be categorized into automated and semi-automated methods. Semi-automated approaches involve the builder of the process workflows creating a reference model, which is compared to the actual process data to generate a validated model. A recent method compares the actual process to a reference model by utilizing a declarative language, but it only produces a comparison of the two models and their corresponding variables. Our research builds upon this comparison by extending the declarative language to include queries and declarations on data, which enables the monitoring and exploration of actual process data in relation to the reference model. This extension ensures that declarations on data are consistent with the actual process data, and it includes a declaration for valid values of data, as well as a declaration for the occurrence of data events. Our approach also allows for the declaration of relationships between data and process variables, and it includes a declarative approach for handling errors and deviations in the actual process. Furthermore, our approach provides for the declaration of data values as sources and as targets, and it includes a declarative approach for handling the duration and timing of the actual process.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden shift from localization to non-localization. Our theory and experimental results indicate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light localization can transition back to non-localization at higher quasiperiodic modulation strengths, a phenomenon we term the "reentrant delocalization shift". This occurrence is specifically related to the interplay between two different quasiperiodic states and can provide a foundation for developing strategies to prevent or exploit wave localization.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. However, Liger's data complexity necessitates a tailored data processing system to refine its output in real-time for effective use with PAFS. We outline the data processing system's design and explain how the system's components and protocol will enable seamless communication with PAFS software.

A major limitation in the scalability of quantum computing and advanced telecommunications lies in the capability to manage the modes of an arbitrary laser pulse entering a quantum network. One method to overcome this challenge is through the separation of the spatial modes carried by two photons produced by a single light source. Although this technique has been successfully demonstrated in various settings, the precision of the mode separation is currently restricted by the minimum resolvable distance between the modes, which needs to be significantly reduced to achieve full control over the system. Here, we present a novel approach that employs machine learning to analyze the correlation of the photon pairs' patterns, enabling the accurate identification of the modes without the need for coherent information about the state of the system. This method excels over existing solutions by utilizing only twice the amount of incoherent data required by conventional methods, while achieving a nearly three times improvement in the resolution limit. Furthermore, our experiment demonstrates that this technique can effectively handle the complex patterns produced by a laser beam passed through a photonic fiber, allowing for mode separation with an accuracy of $0.3\lambda/\sqrt{N}$, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength of the light and $N$ is the number of spatial modes.
This paper investigates both algebraic and analytic extensions of moduli spaces of analytic functions from a domain in the complex plane to a given variety.

In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the specific timeframes over which subtle changes become statistically significant are crucial objectives. This research focuses on a two-timescale ecosystem model, where the dynamics of an ecosystem are influenced by slow-moving species that graze on large plants and fast-moving species that are drawn to small plants. The model's complexity leads to a Gaussian distribution of fitted parameters, which in turn produces a mixed-effects distribution. The model's performance is evaluated during a relatively short quasi-stationary period to ensure the accuracy of its predictions over a longer period. The results show that the model accurately predicts major population changes and the associated timeframes for at least three to four times the period of quasi-stationarity. However, the model's ability to predict early warning signs of major population changes in the long term is still unknown. Therefore, this study proposes a new approach based on the model's performance during a short period of strong variation, and investigates its performance over a longer period to determine the efficacy of this approach. The results show that the model is effective in predicting early warning signs of major population changes in the long term, and identify specific timeframes and early warning indicators for this prediction. Furthermore, the model's performance is compared with alternative methods based on raw and transformed data.

We investigated the standard far-infrared SFR indicator versus stellar mass relation, observed at high masses to turn over instead of following the expected correlation predicted by theoretical models. Using a comprehensive dataset that includes nearby spirals and gas-rich early-type discs, we employed a method to separate the nuclear region from the rest of the galaxy. We found that the traditional one-size-fits-all approach overestimates the star formation in galaxies with nuclear activity by over 100 times their typical contribution in inactive galaxies. Furthermore, we discovered that the predicted relation holds true for the bulk galaxy mass, excluding nuclear regions. These findings suggest that the apparent turning over of the relation at high masses is likely due to the unusually enhanced star formation in nuclear regions of massive galaxies.

This paper focuses on cross-language sentiment analysis, where the task is to classify the emotion behind news headlines in multiple languages. We selected nine languages for this task and built a multi-task learning model to achieve it. Since each language has a limited amount of labeled data, our model incorporated two key elements to enhance performance. Firstly, it utilized character-level embeddings to accommodate languages that use non-Latin scripts, thus leveraging the basic features of characters across different languages. Secondly, it leveraged the inherent similarities between languages by implementing a shared hidden layer in the neural network. Our model showed a notable improvement in classification accuracy on an extensive dataset consisting of 9 languages, specifically achieving the highest score to date on the SemEval 2017 Task 4.

Concurrent programs that incorporate threads and locks can exhibit significant
performance gains, yet they introduce the challenge of synchronisation-related
bugs. To address this, this paper presents a novel technique called self-downgrade
validation (SDV), which complements self-invalidations (SIs) in locking systems.
The SI approach has already been proven to identify a single conflicting thread
within an O(log n) lock-hopping time, where n represents the number of locks.
Building on this, the SDV technique is demonstrated to pinpoint all conflicting
threads in O(log n) time. The proposed SDV algorithm is all-encompassing,
as it can be applied to various SI implementations, including those employing
indirect points-to data structures and array-based locks. The development of
SDV is grounded in an empirical study, which motivates this novel technique.
The study's findings suggest that SI tools often fail to detect synchronisation
errors due to upgrade conflicts in real-world applications. As a result, the SDV
technique is presented as a potential solution to address this limitation. The
implementation and evaluation of SDV are also discussed in the context of the
existing SI approach. As such, the proposed SDV framework offers the capacity
to repair fences in conjunction with SIs, thereby providing a foundation for
future exploration and development of program analysers.

In 2001, Greedy and Kolesnik published a proof of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem for subsets of integers with a additive diameter of less than or equal to 2. This publication was followed by various expansions and a broader application to sets with higher sum-distributions by the authors and others. Recently, Coglatere and Szegedy built upon earlier work by Junor, showcasing an essentially short proof of the 3k-4 theorem that doesn't rely on polynomial methods. In this sequence of developments, we would like to present a new proof based on a specific application of semi-efficient testing for 3-color sumsets, which can be used to prove more complex cases beyond Freiman's 3k-4 theorem.

Consider a fractional Brownian motion $B^{H}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with Hurst index $H$ in the interval $(0,1)$. Let $f$ be a Borel function from $[0,1]$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and $A$ a Borel subset of $[0,1]$. Conditions will be established under which the image $(f)\circ B^{H}$ has a positive Lebesgue measure or a non-empty interior. This is achieved through investigating properties of the set $(f)\circ B^{H}$ by using results from regularity properties of stochastic integrals.

Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we establish a simple H\'enon-Heiles model based on semiclassical mechanics. A two-body trial wavefunction in the form of Hatree-type is applied, leading to the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian in the context of Jackiw-Kerman theory. The calculations yield predictable outcomes, including the determination of an expected energy value that correlates with the characteristics of confined motion and rotational states within the H\'enon-Heiles system.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with the potential to influence COVID-19 patient outcomes following intensive care unit (ICU) admission. By combining medical imaging analysis and statistical risk assessment, our approach aims to create an early warning system for predicting patients' chances of survival. Instead of focusing on existing diagnosis methods for X-ray images, our strategy involves identifying predictive features from an existing dataset using a machine learning-based approach, with an underlying theory based on mathematical concepts. Specifically, we use multifunctional tools to extract features from images and generalized models to evaluate feature importance, with an ultimate goal of optimizing the selection of predictive image characteristics. By choosing features that minimize noise and maximize predictive accuracy, our approach can potentially create an early warning system for predicting patients' survival probabilities.

The notion of a universal simplicial collection has been recently introduced, providing a simplicial analogue of the concept of a universal bundle. However, it is not immediately apparent that the universal simplicial collection is related to the simplicial simplicification functors. By establishing this relationship, we demonstrate that the universal simplicial collection is, in fact, a simplicial group that embeds in a simplicial automorphism of the simplicial simplicification functors. This embedding is achieved through a process involving the use of simplicial Baranovitch extension functors.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of erroneous positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection.

This study offers a supervised action recognition classification model called R-BERT, which is designed to operate with limited and poorly lit video data. The proposed R-BERT is a variant of BERT that incorporates delta sampling, allowing it to learn from restricted data. The model is challenged to classify human activities from low-quality and inadequately lit video in the evaluation phase. The results show that R-BERT outperforms other comparison models.

This project introduces a novel concept called Content Addressable Concurrent Processors, a groundbreaking model that allows multiple processing units to simultaneously examine memory content based on pattern matches. From a technical standpoint, this model is a groundbreaking interpretation of the content-addressable memory idea, pioneered by Bernard Widrow in 1970. Our implementation of this model utilizes Field-Programmable Gate Arrays and combines two core components: a content-addressable memory module and a processor unit. The memory module, designed for high pattern-matching speeds, utilizes a combination of regular and direct matches. The processor unit, capable of executing basic arithmetic operations and logical operations, can also perform context switching and I/O operations. Furthermore, we have an example application demonstrating a PACF with four processing units and 256 memory cells, and through practical testing, we have proven the effectiveness of our design.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling it towards their core. Furthermore, we observe that disk asymmetry is associated with gas streams that are feeding the galaxies and influencing their evolution. This is manifested by an aligned major-axis of galaxies in relation to nearby filaments, presenting observational evidence of accretion streams on galaxy evolution. This is demonstrated by bulge construction, combined with massive quiescent, lopsided galaxies in the current stage, until they collide with a major merger galaxy.

We investigate how accurately a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analysis can determine the parameters of a model using a simple, effective model for neutrino oscillation. To speed up the calculation, we approximate the likelihood function with a Gaussian distribution, relating the uncertainty of the parameter findings to the size of the step size in the MCMC. By comparing the results of rigorous neutrino oscillation simulations with those from our simplified method, we identify the achievable precision of the parameter findings. Furthermore, we examine how increasing the energy range and number of virtual processes in the simulations affect the accuracy. Additionally, we explore the unique features of the model, specifically the universal texture zero of flavor, which could be confirmed or refuted with high confidence at next-generation long-baseline neutrino experiments like Drell-Yan.

We investigate a specific nonlinear elliptic equation that models the formation of boilers in natural convection, given by $\Delta u+\lambda f(u)\delta_{\lambda}(x)-\epsilon=0$, where $\lambda$ represents the Perelman functional and $\delta_{\lambda}(x)$ is a smoothed Dirac delta function. Notably, we prove the existence of a broad range of solutions, including those that are periodic, as well as demonstrating the uniqueness of solutions within a specific, local context. Additionally, we establish the relationship between the sign of $\lambda$ and the solutions' behavior, showing that periodic solutions are indicated by $\lambda$ being positive.

Current cutting-edge neural program generators are highly effective but often rely on comprehensive and high-quality datasets that describe expected output for each input and corresponding code. Unfortunately, they struggle to generalize well to novel instances based on static program characteristics, which are easily extracted but may not necessarily reflect producible code. To address this limitation, we propose an innovative approach that combines a data-driven method for creating new programs with analysis of their underlying code. This static program analysis helps identify acceptable input patterns by mining successful program inputs, which inform a neural-based generator to produce new, feasible code based on these patterns. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through two applications: generating new Python functions and creating new Java method combinations. Our results show that our method outperforms industry-leading baselines in both cases.

Recently discovered solar neutron observations from mountaintop laboratories and commercial aircraft offer new insights into the field, complementing space-based measurements. We examine Nov 7, 2004 particle data from the University of Minnesota's mountaintop laboratory in Arizona, reporting previously unpublished findings. Our analysis includes particle energy measurements, latency estimates, and Latency-to-Flux relationships, in addition to geological event associations. We also compare these results to existing space-based data from the University of Minnesota's flight laboratory and the National Aeronautic and Space Administration's (NASA) spacecraft.

The first order relativistic hydrodynamic model is a straightforward derivation from a second order viscous fluid model, based on a linearized fluid relation that can be a choice of first order hydrodynamic models. By distinguishing first order and second order approximations in our analysis, we determine the specific conditions under which the first order hydrodynamics models are consistent with each other, given that they all lead to the same second order approximation. Additionally, we find that these models can be distinguished through linear perturbations of plane waves, specifically in their dissipation and distortion behaviors. Notably, our analysis finds that the equation of state holds strictly in first order approximations.

Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum walks, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams.

A pivotal question arises when a citizen's privacy clashes with a government agency's investigative needs. To address this, we propose a novel approach, dubbed 'DDF,' which stands for Decryption via Device Fixity. This approach leverages a cutting-edge technique from code obfuscation, namely 'code motion,' to create an implementation detail that agency surveillance can detect. However, this detection is achieved without revealing any valuable information that could be used for malicious purposes. Furthermore, we explore code motion's potential as a solution by developing a practical application using DDF. Specifically, we design a practical framework for its application, providing a working prototype and conducting a comprehensive security evaluation for it. Moreover, we deliberate on the ethical implications and broader implications of code motion in the context of encryption and decryption.

We have established a comprehensive model that enables simulation of the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) process. This model can be applied to evaluate real-world implementations of MDI-QKD based on actual measurement data from laboratory settings or real-world applications. Furthermore, with this model, the key rate achieved in real-world implementations can be compared to the optimal performance of corresponding theoretical scenarios.

On the basis of a new quasi-PTAS, a PTAS can be developed for certain integer optimization problems that contain general-valued objectives and have a specific sparsity level. This breakthrough represents a significant expansion of previous findings which were limited to problems with uniformly represented objective functions. Instead, the new approach allows the representation of objectives using an arbitrary function that can be compared to a given integer within a specific range. This achievement is made possible by the development of a new algorithm based on the Berman-Chen method and its application to clustering problems, while the quasi-PTAS was inspired by the recent APX-hard classification of general-valued Max-Cut problems.

This study presents a novel, high-order numerical approach for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under a constant diffusion term. The devised method integrates elements from the Lagrange-Galerkin and semi-Lagrangian techniques, yielding an explicit, conservative, consistent, and robust scheme capable of handling substantial time step sizes. A convergence analysis for the exactly integrated Lagrange-Galerkin approach is provided, along with an implementable alternative that employs approximate integration. The method is particularly useful in modeling time-dependent mean field games systems, enabling high-order solution approximations.

Advancements in machine learning and signal processing have generated substantial interest in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), which excel at solving complex, engineering-driven problems. Nonetheless, the complexity of these networks hinders their understanding through normal network visualization methods. Various novel techniques have emerged to address this knowledge gap by providing intuitive representations of the processing mechanisms underlying DNNs. This study surveys innovative approaches to elucidating the operation of these networks through computational models and graphical representations.

The findings from previous research on the spinning surface of FGK stars are examined, suggesting that many stars exhibit greater rotational velocities than expected, potentially due to planetary systems, while others may have more manageable theories, such as angular momentum redistribution through tidal interactions with small bodies or the breaking of equatorial long-wavelength sound waves. It is observed that stars with short orbital periods for their size tend to have higher rotational velocities more easily explained by planetary consumption, while those with longer periods require alternative explanations. However, even in the former group, angular momentum redistribution might still be at play, and interacting binaries display unusually high rotational velocities that cannot be attributed to planetary consumption or magnetic mechanisms.

The rapid dissemination of information on social media has made it challenging to detect false news soon after its emergence. We introduce a novel false news detection framework that incorporates multiple data sources, including news content and user behavior, and is trained with a Meta Neural Process Networks architecture. This framework leverages meta-learning to develop a fast-adapting model that can effectively utilize small amounts of emergent data and incorporate general knowledge from more typical instances. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework by conducting experiments on the Faggin Dataset, and our results show that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our method achieves a notable improvement in performance on emergent false news, showcasing its capability to handle time-sensitive tasks.

This paper examines a transport equation featuring cyclic velocity field $v_k$, specifically $f_t + f_y + v_k \alpha_t \delta(y - \alpha_t) + v_k \beta_t \delta(y - \beta_t) = 0$, with initial conditions $\alpha(0) = \alpha_0$, $\beta(0) = \beta_0$, and without any a priori bounds on the solution, with the goal of identifying the singularities that develop over time. It is demonstrated that when the velocity field $v_k$ is continuously differentiable, solutions will always become singular at $\alpha_t = \beta_t$ for $t > 0$, and this singularity develops into a sharp gradient in a short period of time. Additionally, the lower bound on the time it takes for a singularity to occur after $t=0$ can be estimated when $v_k$ is a polynomial.

This paper investigates the age of information (AoI) in a discrete-time status updating system that employs the Ber/G/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that utilizing a two-dimensional state vector which simultaneously monitors AoI and packet age enables derivation of the stationary AoI distribution via analysis of a constituted stochastic process. We present the general formula for the AoI distribution and derive an explicit expression for geometrically distributed service times. A comparison between discrete and continuous AoI is provided, including mean values for the M/M/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that the standard queueing theory is capable of analyzing the discrete AoI, outperforming previously proposed methods for continuous time systems.

This work delves into various quantum algebras that arise from a special type of set-theoretic solution to the Yang-Baxter equation and their 'q-analogue' counterparts, also providing common characteristics that these algebras share in terms of quasi-bialgebras and twists. By establishing that set-theoretic and q-analogue solutions produce the same specific types of algebras and by identifying additional constraints for their 'q-deformed' counterparts, this research greatly expands our current understanding of set-theoretic solutions and their quantum equivalents, revealing new general patterns in the field.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained significance due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional complex-valued arrays, comprising multiple frequency bands and directional patterns. A set of four-quadrant Golay complementary arrays is designed in this study, where each array covers 360 degrees and has a size of 32x32. The designed arrays exhibit equal power distribution across all frequency bins and directional patterns. Moreover, they are susceptible to minimal interference. To facilitate implementation, a method for reconstructing larger-sized Golay complementary arrays from their smaller-sized counterparts is also proposed.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atomic arrays.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin-swap operation, outstretching its applicability beyond combined harmonic potentials.
As combined harmonic potentials are commonplace in chemical systems, this finding has significant implications for molecular quantum computing.
In addition, this study demonstrates the potential of silicon-based quantum computing to tackle intricate issues like the quantum driving of chemical reactions over extended distances.
A hypothetical silicon-based quantum computer design is discussed in this study to facilitate the precise execution of Heisenberg's spin-swap operation in silicon.
In this model, the quantum state of He-like silicon ions is controlled by applying a coherent pulse to a coupled $^3$P$_2$ triplet state.
The performance of this quantum processor is assessed by running a series of benchmark programs.
A $42$-qubit version of the quantum processor demonstrates stable operation under various conditions and can execute certain applications significantly faster than its classical counterparts.

Complex systems consisting of interrelated components undergo natural transformations, following universal principles, and exhibit consistent patterns despite appearing random. However, accurately capturing their evolution and underlying structure in a coherent framework has been a significant challenge for scientists across disciplines. In our study, we synthesized 55 years of research on graph theory, network analysis, and time series prediction, leveraging multiple tools and techniques such as graph neural networks, nonlinear filters, and statistical analysis. Our integrated approach, involving multiple components, can detect subtle changes in a complex system's dynamics, identify specific patterns, and extract valuable information from raw data, ultimately producing a unified framework and providing a platform for future research and exploration.

We introduce a family of integer sequences V_d that represent the counts of specific partition configurations, which are inherently linked to elements of a particular type in the homotopy theory of symmetric monoids. These sequences exhibit intriguing patterns when D is a prime number, displaying both periodic behavior and links to well-known number sequences like the M\"obius function and binomial coefficients. Our findings also reveal a connection to the Euler phi function, which isn't immediately apparent. This connection arises from a broader framework involving the homotopy type of symmetric monoids and their connections to category theory via the concept of polynomial functors.

Our proposal utilizes a progressive variational auto-encoder with adversarial components to create realistic images of brain injuries from limited and poorly quality X-ray images. A specific design was adopted for the encoder and decoder components, utilizing convolutional neural network architecture, while also incorporating a convolutional decoder to generate injury images. The quality of these generated images was assessed using both quantitative and qualitative evaluation methods. Our research demonstrates the potential for autoencoders to create realistic injury images from limited X-ray data, facilitating advanced applications such as trauma classification and detection.

Recent advancements in quantum communication have spurred significant interest in unextendible product bases (UPBs) as a reliable tool for investigating quantum nonlocality in multiparty systems. UPBs pose an interesting challenge because any set of entangled states must necessarily be coherent to exhibit nonlocal properties, yet certain UPBs in heterogeneous systems may contain highly robust quantum nonlocality. To thoroughly comprehend the quantum nonlocality inherent in these bases, we developed a novel approach to evaluate the steering capacity of UPBs, effectively allowing us to determine the capacity of a UPB to exhibit nonlocal behavior when a portion of its states are replaced by an attack from an arbitrary environment. Using this approach, we investigated the robust quantum nonlocality present in UPBs in heterogeneous systems, including those composed of systems with descriptions of space (e.g., $M_A \otimes M_B \otimes \cdots$), as well as systems with descriptions of time (e.g., $M_A^{\otimes n} \otimes M_B^{\otimes n}$). Furthermore, we proposed a straightforward method for creating UPBs with robust quantum nonlocality in systems with descriptions of time, as well as a novel approach for examining the relationship between the size of a UPB and its robust quantum nonlocality, potentially leading to further study of UPBs with optimal robust quantum nonlocality.

The speed at which massive spectroscopic surveys collect data directly corresponds to the number of optical fibers used in each observation. This paper examines the effectiveness and efficiency of a method for coordinating astrobots in the SDSS-V by running numerous simulated and real-world tests. We demonstrate that our approach establishes a complete coordination framework based on the specific features and configurations of astrobots, their objectives, and operating parameters. Additionally, our results show that this method yields the most optimal combinations, often uniquely, when faced with a large number of available fibers relative to stars, especially in scenarios mimicking the SDSS main area and featuring a high star density. However, the algorithm performs best when the number of available fibers exceeds the number of stars by at least five to ten times.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, we incorporated a novel approach into the GP 2 compiler, replacing traditional matching methods with more robust and faster alternatives. This enhanced compiler, developed in collaboration with the GP 2 toolchain, can compile programs featuring efficient match operations, thereby speeding up analysis and verification processes.

In recent years, the success of contrastive learning in group settings has been evident, essentially viewing data preparation as an organization problem. This approach has led to significant advancements in supervised feature extraction projects, allowing for the use of pre-trained models as high-performing classifiers in scenarios where the target dataset is known. Building upon contrastive learning's foundation, a novel, unified structure for feature extraction has been proposed, incorporating a novel cluster loss function to achieve contrastive learning in an one-to-one mapping scenario. This structure's efficacy is demonstrated across real-world datasets, showcasing superior performance compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the proposed structure's adaptability is examined in scenarios where the target labels are unknown, leading to novel insights on contrastive learning's relationship with self-organizing maps and multidimensional scaling.

We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved high performance in various tasks, exhibiting a capacity for leveraging structured information to inform their predictions. In response, researchers have initiated structured knowledge injection techniques to enhance the capabilities of these models. While initial approaches have yielded promising results, there remains a lack of unified framework addressing the incorporation of structured knowledge into transformer-based models. To address this gap, we present a unified framework called SKILL, which enables the efficient integration of structured information into large language models through multi-head structured attention layers. The framework effectively facilitates the incorporation of diverse structured data formats, including graphs and tables, thereby enhancing the model's capacity for understanding and applying structured knowledge. The efficacy of SKILL is demonstrated through the enhancement of LLMs using various knowledge graphs, as well as comparisons with alternative baselines in the context of few-shot conjecture verification and math word problems. The code for SKILL is made publicly available, offering a versatile knowledge injection framework that models can draw upon.

Our research develops comprehensive fractional diffusion frameworks, incorporating spatial nonlocality, in a bounded domain with various boundary conditions. These models can be specialized to match well-known local equations such as Laplace, Poiseuille, and Cahn-Hilliard equations. We specifically explore fractional versions of the Laplace equation with constant and spatially-dependent coefficients, time-dependent Poiseuille flows, and a Cahn-Hilliard type equation. Our study addresses existence, uniqueness, and Regge calculus stability for the resulting fractional equations. Additionally, we investigate the appropriateness of different fractional operators and their impact on the model's behavior.

When creating panoramic images, we take multiple photos while moving around a steady axis, thus requiring precise estimation of that axis. This process is complicated by uncertain pose measurements, which necessitate a robust algorithm to work effectively. We can obtain a precise axis estimation by employing a suitable algorithm and sufficient, well-positioned images. However, when the number of images is limited, as is often the case with panoramic photos, obtaining accurate axis estimations becomes even more challenging due to the effects of pose uncertainties. We have investigated ways to minimize the requirements for such images, taking account of the direction of gravity, and found that two views under certain lighting conditions are sufficient for solving this problem. We have also developed a novel algorithm to achieve this minimal requirement, demonstrating its efficacy through practical applications.

Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series combinatorics has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the automation of the Newburger and Shahidi procedure 
for $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$.

This study develops a novel biophysical model of brain dysfunction associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing computational neuroscience methods and data from marmoset monkey brains. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal dopaminergic transmission between the marmoset monkey's substantia nigra and striatum. To model this disorder, a 3-dimensional model of the marmoset monkey's substantia nigra and surrounding areas was created using a combination of blue brain technology and the Nernst-Plangeckoff equations. Models of healthy and Parkinson's disease-affected brains were then compared, revealing the impact of neuronal death on local field potential and the transmission of dopaminergic signals. Furthermore, an investigation into the effectiveness of deep brain stimulation in the marmoset monkey brain is also presented. Computational neuroscience approaches, including spiking neuronal networks and multi-electrode recordings, were employed to model the disorder's effects on the monkey's cognition and motor skills. Our findings suggest that deep brain stimulation can alleviate the symptoms of Parkinson's disease by transmitting electrical signals into the monkey's brain. To facilitate further exploration of Parkinson's disease models, the developed model is available online for users to modify and replicate the results.

The integration of graphic rendering and geographic information systems (GIS) is crucial for creating engaging and high-performance map applications. However, there is no widely adopted, universally applicable framework for rendering line joins, which is a fundamental component of vector maps. To address this issue, we propose a novel, high-performance algorithm for rendering line joins combining spatial anti-aliasing techniques. The proposed method enhances the aesthetic appeal and user experience of map rendering, while also improving performance by reducing unnecessary computation. To demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of this approach, we conducted a series of experiments and adaptations for common map layers, including roads, rivers, and area borders. The proposed algorithm is efficient, easy to implement, and adaptable to various rendering environments and platforms.

Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy.

Cloud categorization holds significant importance in understanding the evolution of clouds, which directly impacts radar wave propagation and ultimately influences radio signal reception. Current methods primarily rely on visual assessments, but these are time-consuming, unreliable, and often biased. A new approach is needed to categorize clouds into four types (pilotable, obstructive, medium-height, and low-lying) to aid pilot safety. This paper introduces the first cloud dataset classified into these four categories and proposes a novel data augmentation technique called spatial-shift transformation, offering promising results with state-of-the-art CNNs. Evaluations of thirteen CNN models on this dataset reveal that our proposed method achieves superior performance, surpassing 90% accuracy with relatively simple networks.

A dual-path model for convolved and reverberant speech restoration has been proposed in a previous study by Wang et al. This model's effectiveness has been widely demonstrated, and it has become a fundamental framework for speech processing. To further improve speech quality, a dual-path convex recurrent network (DPCRN) model has been built upon this foundation. In DPCRN, the dual-path model is applied to separate a noisy signal into convolved and reverberant components, which are then processed through two independent convex recurrent networks. These networks model the non-linear relationships in both categories and have been shown to significantly reduce reverberation in speech. Through comparative evaluations with existing convex and recurrent networks, DPCRN has consistently achieved higher speech quality scores (MOS) in subjective assessments and outperformed them in objective metrics such as SI-DR, SI-SNR, and PESQ.

A new statistics methodology is introduced, focused on the turn-around radii of cluster halos to break the degeneracy between $\Lambda$CDM, alternative $f(R)$ gravity models, and massive neutrinos cosmologies characterized by fifth force strength and total neutrino mass. By analyzing the rockstar halo catalogs at the present epoch from the DUSTGRAIN-pathfinder $N$-body simulations of four distinct cosmologies, including $\Lambda$CDM, fR6, fR6+$0.06$eV, and fR5+$0.15$eV, the method evaluates the probability distribution of ratios between turn-around radii and virial counterparts, effectively distinguishing between these cosmologies. It is found that fR6 and fR5+$0.15$eV can be differentiated by $10\sigma$ difference and $\Lambda$CDM and fR6+$0.06$eV can be differentiated by $3.2\sigma$ difference. Furthermore, the models exhibit decreasing differences in the probability distribution at higher redshifts.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid simulation of Rayleigh-Benard convection, featuring fluid density differences caused by varying temperature. Multiple resolution levels and two different interface-capture techniques have been implemented into the simulation. A basic closure for the interaction between fluids via exchange coefficients is also introduced. Ultimately, the study aims to explore the practical applicability of the multi-fluid approach in conjunction with the use of subgrid-scale interface models in atmospheric convection scenarios.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, where two of the systems have correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. However, through a process involving the exchange of linearized gravitational field fluctuations, it's possible to entangle the unconnected system with the other two. The amount of entanglement that can be created is determined by a quantum version of the maximum likelihood principle.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot blades built using advanced digital readout chips. Through pilot module testing, researchers obtained practical experience with the upgraded detector. This study reports the results of analyzing data captured with these new components, including a detailed explanation of the reconstruction process and associated calibration steps. Furthermore, it includes illustrations of the hit finding efficiency and track-hit residual patterns.

A method is presented for computing the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral density from lattice QCD data, which remains gauge invariant. The proposed method is tested on a model of SU(2) gluonium scalar form factors using both numerical and analytical approaches. Further investigation is also conducted on the spectral density's angular dependence and corresponding spectral densities for different polarisation states. These studies are relevant for the Lattice QCD collaboration's efforts to measure SU(2) gluonium spectral functions.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

This research investigates the thermodynamic properties of a non-linear, charged AdS black hole under the influence of a linear shade field. The team employs a new, linearized non-linear field transformation to analyze the thermodynamics and uncover the critical features of the black hole's phase transition. Using a semi-analytical method, they identify the phase transition boundaries and create detailed diagrams of the thermodynamic behavior in both the shade-free and shade-influenced scenarios. Additionally, this study expands our understanding of the impact of the shade field on the thermodynamic behavior of non-linear, charged AdS black holes.

The tomographic technique offers a comprehensive understanding of quantum states through its reconstruction of the density matrix. This state reconstruction can provide insights into the entanglement properties of a continuous-variable system. A new representation of tomograms is based on the Wigner function, which enables the visualization of quantum correlations, including when they become soliton-like. By analyzing these tomograms and their associated spectra, we can identify the rates of soliton separation as well as the onset of soliton synchronization, which can be demonstrated through numerical examples.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features like persona, role, or goal.
To tackle this issue, our work proposes an innovative approach that utilizes large language models for both training and evaluation.
In this approach, we utilize large language models to train role-specific dialogue models through bidirectional knowledge distillation.
To facilitate efficient training, we introduce a novel multi-task knowledge distillation framework that combines role-aware knowledge distillation and language modeling objectives.
Furthermore, we introduce the Role-Specified Dialogue State Tracker to ensure the learned model meets role specifications during conversation.
Empirical evaluations on a dataset annotated for role, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in constructing a role-specific chat system.

Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing average treatment benefits and risks. Evaluating pesticide efficacy using certainty equivalents and ranking treatment efficiency through stochastic efficiency is a common practice. However, the major drawback of this approach is collecting a sufficient number of observations for statistically meaningful results. Since field experiments typically have a limited number of replicated trials, the results lack sufficient data. Moreover, the conventional method solely considers farmer profitability, disregarding the influence of disease pressure on yields and profit. To address these challenges, we developed a method using simulations to account for a limited number of observations and incorporated disease pressure's effect through a quantile regression model, applying this solution to strawberry disease management in Florida.

360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences, but presenting their audio is more complicated due to potential misalignment between video and audio. This problem is particularly pronounced in video descriptions, which often inaccurately reflect the audio, causing disorientation in viewers. To address this issue, we propose a novel task of predicting viewers' perspectives based on video subtitles. Our research incorporates multi-task learning and the use of attention mechanisms to minimize the difference between the encoding of subtitles and the estimation of perspective. This is represented mathematically as a self-supervised learning problem, which we resolve through contrastive training. Our models, along with associated modifications and extensions, are tested on datasets obtained from YouTube and Findus, resulting in superior performance and comprehensive, practical applications.

Tensor network methods have commonly been applied to model both equilibrium and nonequilibrium situations, with two main types of approximations: tensor network architectures that generally apply to systems at equilibrium and those that can be locally accurate in nonequilibrium situations. This work focuses on developing tensor network objects that can capture the stochastic nature of quantum systems in both thermal states and time-evolved situations. The resulting objects serve as the fundamental building blocks for implementing various tensor network algorithms, such as the time-dependent variational renal density functional theory, the dynamical density matrix renormalization group, and the thermal renormalization group. We demonstrate our tensor networks' efficiency by applying them to a nonequilibrium model featuring a quantum quench and a light-matter system. The development of these tensor networks also enables the direct computation of physical observables via their associated expectation values.

We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of restricted efficacy from one-dimensional applications to three-dimensional scenarios. As a result, we derive a significant breakthrough in our research, enabling the development of new approximate formulas using an average value method. These formulas provide a general solution, applying to any positive $\delta$ less than one. Moreover, we establish a relationship between our decoupling technique and the method of scale-based approximations. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of both methods by applying them to specific surfaces, including rational functions and polynomial surfaces with irrational roots.

In this research, we establish an anisotropic $p$-capacitance inequality, building upon the anisotropic Minkowski inequality. Specifically, let $K$ be a compact, convex set in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and $f$ a convex function defined on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then, the Anisotropic Minkowski Inequality states that $$f\left(\frac{1}{|K|}\int_K x d\lambda^{\mathbb{R}^n}(x)\right)\leq \frac{1}{|K|}\int_K f(x) d\lambda^{\mathbb{R}^n}(x).$$Our main result expands upon this by showing that for any compact, convex set $K$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and any convex function $f$ defined on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the following Anisotropic $p$-capacitance inequality holds: $$\left(\int_K |x|^p d\lambda^{\mathbb{R}^n}(x)\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}\leq \left(\frac{1}{|K|}\int_K |x|^p d\lambda^{\mathbb{R}^n}(x)\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}\cdot |B_1^p|,$$

The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This experiment was designed to minimize potential errors at these critical frequencies. Unforeseen events known as glitches can occur during data collection, affecting the test's results. These events, which remain largely uncharacterized, can stem from a variety of sources such as cosmic radiation, power fluctuations, or mechanical issues with the satellite. While glitches generally have a minor impact on the test, it's essential to understand their full effect. This calculation takes into account not just the glitches themselves, but also the resulting slight adjustments to the satellite's orientation and its orbital path. This adjustment causes slight fluctuations in the frequency tests are designed for, which in turn affects the test's results. This specific calculation considers all past glitches encountered by the Microscope test and provides a statistical breakdown of their impact, which in total amounts to roughly one-quarter of the test's achievable precision.

The movement of suspended particles is influenced by fluid flow and their own interactions, which can lead to complex patterns of motion. When the particles interact in such a way that they form a 'dumbbell' shape with an asymmetrical activity level, it affects their stability and behavior in a flowing fluid, particularly near an area where the flow speed changes. This study uses advanced computer simulations to examine how the stability and movement of these colloidal molecules vary depending on the level of activity and flow conditions. The results show that increasing activity or flow speed can lead to instability and biased movement. Furthermore, in conditions of moderate activity and flow, these particles can be controlled to move in a specific direction by adjusting the asymmetry of their shape. This phenomenon is linked to changes in the particles' orientation over time, which create a'memory effect' and influence their movement in subsequent stages.

The minimum k-path problem in a graph requires determining the smallest collection of k paths whose edges overlap in a specific manner, particularly where the sum of any k paths excludes edges with a certain property. This paper explores various paradigms related to the minimum k-path problem, including finding the smallest collection of k paths meeting a certain criterion, as well as the k-strong shortest path problem, which involves identifying the shortest collection of k paths with no overlap in a specific manner. This study specifically considers graphs that are planar, outerplanar, tree-like, and dual graph structures, as well as general graphs and their connected components.
